explanation: Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are benign, slow-growing tumors arising from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve (CN VIII), typically at the junction of central and peripheral myelin (Obersteiner-Redlich zone) within the internal acoustic meatus and cerebellopontine angle (CPA). Initial symptoms are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vestibular unsteadiness. As the tumor expands into the CPA, it compresses adjacent cranial nerves: CN VII (facial weakness) and CN V (loss of corneal reflex and facial numbness).
high_yield_pearl: Vestibular Schwannoma: Benign Schwann cell tumor of CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle -> unilateral SNHL, tinnitus, loss of corneal reflex (CN V).

source: Content Q8: Ototoxicity Mechanisms
question: A 63-year-old patient with severe sepsis is treated with intravenous amikacin and high-dose intravenous furosemide. Five days into therapy, the patient complains of constant ringing in both ears (tinnitus) and severe balance disturbance. By which distinct mechanisms do aminoglycosides and loop diuretics induce inner ear damage?

options.text: Aminoglycosides block acetylcholine receptors in Heschl's gyrus; loop diuretics ablate the medial geniculate body
Aminoglycosides cause toxic reactive oxygen species death of outer hair cells; loop diuretics disrupt ion transport in the stria vascularis
Aminoglycosides calcify the tympanic membrane; loop diuretics induce aseptic osteomyelitis of the incus
Aminoglycosides destroy Schwann cell myelin along the cochlear nerve; loop diuretics paralyze the stapedius muscle
Aminoglycosides trigger autoimmune destruction of the cupula; loop diuretics cause otoconia detachment in the utricle

explanation: Aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin, streptomycin) generate toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) and enter sensory hair cells via mechanotransduction channels, causing irreversible apoptotic death of hair cells (outer hair cells damaged before inner hair cells; vestibular hair cells also affected). Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid) inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC1) in the stria vascularis of the cochlea, disrupting endolymph generation and causing edema and loss of the endocochlear potential (often reversible). Co-administration produces severe synergistic ototoxicity.
high_yield_pearl: Ototoxicity: Aminoglycosides = ROS damage to outer hair cells (irreversible). Loop diuretics = inhibit NKCC1 in stria vascularis (synergistic).

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 6-9 & Content Q1: Semicircular Canal Physiology
question: The vestibular labyrinth contains three semicircular canals arranged orthogonally in three perpendicular planes. What is the precise mechanical stimulus detected by the hair cells within the ampullary crest (crista ampullaris) of these canals?

options.text: Static gravitational force acting on the body in the upright vertical posture
Angular acceleration and rotational movements of the head in three-dimensional space
High-frequency sound pressure waves traveling through the perilymphatic duct
Linear horizontal acceleration during forward motion in a motor vehicle
Changes in atmospheric barometric pressure transmitted across the round window

explanation: The three semicircular canals (horizontal/lateral, anterior/superior, and posterior) are arranged at right angles to one another. Each canal has a dilated end called the ampulla, which houses the crista ampullaris. Hair cells in the crista project their stereocilia into a gelatinous sail-like membrane called the cupula that spans the entire lumen. When the head undergoes angular acceleration (rotation), endolymph inertia causes fluid flow relative to the canal walls, deflecting the cupula and bending the stereocilia toward or away from the kinocilium to modulate firing rates.
high_yield_pearl: Semicircular canals (crista ampullaris & cupula): Detect ANGULAR acceleration (head rotation in 3 planes).

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 10-11 & Content Q1: Otolith Organs (Utricle & Saccule)
question: Unlike the semicircular canals, the otolith organs (the utricle and saccule) detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity. How does the presence of dense calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) enable the maculae to detect these mechanical forces in endolymph?

options.text: Otoconia buffer potassium ions in the endolymph to prevent hair cell hyperpolarization during rapid movement
Otoconia synthesize and secrete neurotrophin-3 to maintain survival of primary vestibular ganglion cells
Otoconia act as acoustic resonators that amplify low-frequency sound waves entering the vestibule
Otoconia give the otolithic membrane high mass and density, so gravity and linear inertia displace the membrane across the hair cells
Otoconia generate piezoelectric electrical currents that activate voltage-gated calcium channels directly

explanation: The utricle and saccule contain sensory receptor organs called maculae. The stereocilia of macular hair cells are embedded in a gelatinous otolithic membrane topped with thousands of dense calcium carbonate stones called otoconia (otoliths). Because endolymph has a specific gravity near 1.0, a simple gelatinous membrane would be buoyant and insensitive to gravity. The dense otoconia give the membrane substantial mass and inertia: when the head tilts or undergoes linear acceleration (horizontal in utricle, vertical in saccule), the heavy otolithic membrane slides across the underlying hair cells, shearing their stereocilia.
high_yield_pearl: Otolith organs (utricle = horizontal, saccule = vertical/gravity): Dense calcium carbonate otoconia allow detection of LINEAR acceleration & head tilt.

source: Content Q14 & Case 2: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
question: A 66-year-old woman reports recurrent episodes of violent spinning dizziness lasting 20 to 30 seconds that occur whenever she rolls over in bed to her right side or tilts her head back to look at a high shelf. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. Performance of the Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the right side produces intense rotational vertigo and mixed upbeat-torsional nystagmus after a 5-second latency that fatigues after 25 seconds. What is the pathophysiologic mechanism, and what is the definitive management?

options.text: Fistulous communication between the horizontal canal and middle ear; treated with urgent tympanoplasty
Excessive endolymph accumulation causing rupture of the membranous labyrinth; treated with intravenous acetazolamide
Dislodged otoconia from the utricle freely floating in the posterior semicircular canal (canalithiasis); treated with the Epley maneuver
Microvascular compression of the vestibular nerve by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery; treated with surgical decompression
Viral demyelinating inflammation of the vestibular ganglion; treated with high-dose intravenous acyclovir and corticosteroids

explanation: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of peripheral vertigo. It is caused by canalithiasis: calcium carbonate otoconia dislodge from the utricular macula and become trapped in a semicircular canal (most commonly the posterior canal, ~85-90% of cases, due to its gravity-dependent position). Head movement shifts the free-floating debris, creating abnormal endolymph currents that deflect the cupula. Hallmarks on Dix-Hallpike: latency (2-10 seconds), brief duration (<1 minute), torsional upbeat nystagmus, and fatigability upon repeated testing. Definitive treatment is the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver.
high_yield_pearl: BPPV: Posterior canal canalithiasis (dislodged otoconia from utricle). Dix-Hallpike: torsional nystagmus with latency & fatigue. Treat: Epley maneuver.

source: Content Q14 & Case 2: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
question: A 46-year-old man presents with recurrent, disabling episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, roaring left-sided tinnitus, a feeling of 'fullness' and pressure in his left ear, and fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss. Between attacks, his hearing improves significantly. Physical examination during an episode shows horizontal nystagmus beating to the right. What is the underlying pathophysiologic mechanism?

options.text: Erosion of the lateral horizontal semicircular canal bone by an expanding chronic middle ear cholesteatoma mass
Mechanical displacement of otoconia into the anterior semicircular canal following sudden rotational head trauma
Endolymphatic hydrops with excessive accumulation and distension of endolymph within the membranous labyrinth
Autoimmune demyelinating destruction of myelin sheaths surrounding the vestibular root entry zone in the brainstem
Atheroembolic occlusion of the terminal labyrinthine artery arising from the basilar or anterior inferior cerebellar artery

explanation: Meniere's disease (idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops) is caused by impaired resorption or overproduction of endolymph, resulting in progressive swelling and distension of the endolymphatic compartment of the membranous labyrinth. Increased pressure leads to periodic micro-ruptures of the membrane, exposing perilymph to high-potassium endolymph and causing episodic vestibular and cochlear dysfunction. Classic clinical tetrad: 1) Episodic spinning vertigo (lasting 20 min to several hours), 2) Fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, 3) Tinnitus, and 4) Aural fullness. Initial management includes dietary sodium restriction and diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide/triamterene).
high_yield_pearl: Meniere's disease: Endolymphatic hydrops. Classic tetrad: Episodic vertigo (hours) + fluctuating low-frequency SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness. Treat: low-salt diet & diuretics.

source: Case 1 & Content Q14: Vestibular Neuritis
question: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of severe, continuous room-spinning vertigo that began upon waking 24 hours ago. He has severe nausea, multiple bouts of vomiting, and marked unsteadiness, needing to hold onto walls to walk. He had an upper respiratory tract infection one week ago. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus, or headache. Neurological exam reveals spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus with the fast phase beating to the left, which is suppressed when he fixes his gaze on an object. Pure-tone audiometry is completely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Vestibular neuritis involving acute inflammation of the right vestibular nerve
Vertebrobasilar transient ischemic attack causing transient brainstem ischemia
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo affecting the right horizontal semicircular canal
Acute labyrinthitis involving infection of the left cochlea and vestibular apparatus
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory cerebellar ischemic stroke

explanation: Vestibular neuritis is an acute, sustained peripheral vestibulopathy typically presumed to result from post-viral inflammation of the vestibular division of CN VIII (often the superior vestibular nerve). Patients present with acute, severe, continuous spinning vertigo lasting days, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and gait instability. Crucially, auditory function is completely spared (no hearing loss, no tinnitus). Spontaneous unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats AWAY from the affected side (fast phase toward the healthy ear) and is suppressed by visual fixation. A positive head impulse test confirms a peripheral deficit.
high_yield_pearl: Vestibular neuritis: Acute, continuous vertigo + nausea/vomiting + ataxia WITHOUT hearing loss (post-viral CN VIII inflammation). Labyrinthitis has hearing loss.

source: Case 1 & Content Q14: Labyrinthitis
question: A 28-year-old woman recovering from an influenza infection wakes up with sudden, severe continuous vertigo, vomiting, profound left-sided hearing loss, and loud left-sided tinnitus. On examination, she has spontaneous horizontal nystagmus beating to the right and marked difficulty walking. How does labyrinthitis differ pathogenetically and clinically from vestibular neuritis?

options.text: Labyrinthitis involves inflammation of both the cochlear and vestibular divisions, causing hearing loss in addition to vertigo
Labyrinthitis is caused by mechanical displacement of otoconia into the anterior canal without inflammation
Labyrinthitis is confined exclusively to the cerebellum, causing dysmetria without peripheral nystagmus
Labyrinthitis affects only the motor division of the facial nerve, presenting with Bell's palsy
Labyrinthitis involves autoimmune vasculitis of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery branches

explanation: Acute labyrinthitis involves infection or post-viral inflammatory disruption of the entire membranous labyrinth, thereby affecting both the vestibular apparatus and the cochlea (or both divisions of CN VIII). Clinically, it presents identically to vestibular neuritis with acute, incapacitating, continuous vertigo, nausea, and gait imbalance, but it is uniquely distinguished by the presence of unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus in the affected ear.
high_yield_pearl: Labyrinthitis vs. Vestibular Neuritis: Both present with acute prolonged continuous vertigo; Labyrinthitis includes hearing loss/tinnitus; Vestibular Neuritis spares hearing.

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 23-30 & Content Q3: Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR) Arc
question: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) maintains stable retinal images during rapid head movements by rotating the eyes with equal velocity in the direction opposite to head motion. When an individual rapidly turns their head to the LEFT, which neural circuit is activated to drive the compensatory conjugate eye movement to the RIGHT?

options.text: Left horizontal canal -> Left vestibular nucleus -> Right abducens nucleus (via MLF to Left oculomotor nucleus)
Bilateral saccules -> Pontine reticular formation -> Direct activation of both superior oblique muscles
Right horizontal canal -> Right vestibular nucleus -> Left abducens nucleus (via MLF to Right oculomotor nucleus)
Left anterior canal -> Right superior colliculus -> Left trochlear nucleus and medial rectus subnucleus
Left utricle -> Left fastigial nucleus -> Bilateral trochlear nerves through the superior medullary velum

explanation: When the head turns to the LEFT: 1) Endolymph inertia deflects cupula stereocilia toward the kinocilium in the LEFT horizontal canal, increasing firing in the left vestibular nerve. 2) Left vestibular afferents synapse in the left vestibular nuclei. 3) Second-order axons cross the midline to activate the CONTRALATERAL (RIGHT) abducens nucleus (CN VI). 4) Right abducens motor neurons activate the right lateral rectus muscle (abducting right eye). Concurrently, right abducens internuclear neurons project across the midline via the left Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) to the left oculomotor nucleus (CN III) to activate the left medial rectus muscle (adducting left eye). Result: smooth conjugate gaze to the RIGHT.
high_yield_pearl: VOR for Left head turn: Left horizontal canal -> Left vestibular nucleus -> Right CN VI nucleus -> Right lateral rectus + (via left MLF) Left CN III medial rectus.

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 22 & Content Q3: Vestibulospinal Tracts
question: The vestibular nuclei give rise to descending spinal tracts that maintain balance and upright posture against gravity. What is the origin, course, and motor function of the Lateral Vestibulospinal Tract?

options.text: Arises from the superior vestibular nucleus, traverses the lateral funiculus, and coordinates voluntary fine digital movements
Arises from the inferior vestibular nucleus, projects bilaterally to the phrenic nucleus to synchronize diaphragmatic respiration
Arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters), descends uncrossed in the anterior funiculus, and activates extensor antigravity motor neurons
Arises from the medial vestibular nucleus, crosses the midline, and selectively inhibits cervical flexor motor neurons
Arises from the reticular formation, descends within the dorsal columns, and mediates visceral sensory reflexes

explanation: The Lateral Vestibulospinal Tract (LVST) originates predominantly from large neurons in the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters' nucleus) at the pontomedullary junction. It descends uncrossed (ipsilaterally) through the anterior funiculus along the entire length of the spinal cord. It makes excitatory glutamatergic synapses on alpha and gamma motor neurons that innervate axial and limb antigravity extensor muscles (quadriceps, gastrocnemius, back extensors), promoting upright posture and balance in response to linear acceleration and head tilt.
high_yield_pearl: Lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVST): From lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters) -> uncrossed in anterior funiculus -> excites antigravity extensor muscles.

source: Content Q14: Peripheral vs. Central Vertigo
question: A 68-year-old man with hypertension presents with acute dizziness and ataxia. A physician performs a detailed oculomotor examination to differentiate peripheral from central vertigo. Which examination finding is most characteristic of a CENTRAL brainstem or cerebellar lesion rather than a peripheral inner ear disorder?

options.text: Unidirectional nystagmus with the fast phase beating consistently in the same direction across all gazes
Severe rotational vertigo with pronounced autonomic nausea and vomiting
A 5-second latency before the onset of nystagmus and symptoms during positional testing
Presence of purely vertical downbeat nystagmus that does not suppress with visual fixation
Horizontal-torsional nystagmus that is markedly suppressed when the patient fixates on a visual target

explanation: Central vertigo (arising from brainstem or cerebellar pathology such as stroke or demyelination) is distinguished by: 1) Non-suppression of nystagmus by visual fixation (fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus), 2) Purely vertical (downbeat or upbeat) or purely torsional nystagmus (peripheral nystagmus is almost always mixed horizontal-torsional), 3) Direction-changing nystagmus on lateral gaze, 4) Mild nausea relative to severe gait ataxia (patients often cannot stand unassisted), and 5) Absence of latency or fatigability on positional testing.
high_yield_pearl: Central vertigo: Pure vertical nystagmus, direction-changing, NOT suppressed by visual fixation, severe ataxia. Peripheral: suppressed by fixation, fatigable.

source: Content Q6: Cerebellopontine Angle (CPA) Anatomy & Syndrome
question: A 55-year-old man has a large meningioma occupying the right cerebellopontine angle (CPA). The mass compresses the lateral pontomedullary junction and neighboring structures. Which constellation of neurological signs corresponds to compression of the anatomical structures traversing this specific cistern?

options.text: Bilateral bitemporal hemianopia, galactorrhea, hypogonadism, and frontal headache
Paralysis of upward vertical gaze, light-near pupillary dissociation, and convergence-retraction nystagmus
Right sensorineural hearing loss, right peripheral facial weakness, diminished right corneal sensation, and right limb ataxia
Right ptosis, right miosis, right anhidrosis, and hoarseness due to right vocal cord paralysis
Left spastic hemiplegia, left homonymous hemianopia, expressive motor aphasia, and right gaze preference

explanation: The cerebellopontine angle (CPA) is an anatomical cistern between the cerebellum, pons, and petrous temporal bone. Structures passing through or bordering the CPA include: CN VIII (vestibulocochlear: hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo), CN VII (facial: peripheral ipsilateral facial weakness, loss of anterior tongue taste), CN V (trigeminal: loss of ipsilateral corneal reflex and facial sensation), and the middle/inferior cerebellar peduncles (ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia). A mass in this space (e.g., vestibular schwannoma or meningioma) produces this classic CPA syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: Cerebellopontine angle (CPA) syndrome: CN VIII (deafness/vertigo) + CN VII (facial palsy) + CN V (loss of corneal reflex) + Cerebellum (ipsilateral ataxia).

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 30: Caloric Testing & Oculocephalic Reflex
question: Caloric irrigation testing is used to evaluate the integrity of the vestibulo-ocular pathway in an unconscious patient with suspected brainstem injury. When cold water (30 C) is irrigated into the right external auditory canal of a patient in a coma with an intact, functional brainstem, what ocular response is expected?

options.text: Immediate conjugate upward elevation of both globes accompanied by bilateral upper eyelid retraction and spasm
Rapid oscillatory convergence-retraction nystagmus combined with bilateral extraocular muscle abduction failure
Complete pupillary dilation of the right eye accompanied by total loss of the consensual pupillary light reflex
Rapid vigorous horizontal nystagmus with the fast corrective phase beating continuously toward the right ear
Slow conjugate tonic deviation of both eyes toward the irrigated right ear with absence of fast corrective saccades

explanation: Caloric testing stimulates the horizontal semicircular canal via convection currents: cold water cools endolymph, causing it to sink and creating fluid currents away from the ampulla (inhibiting the horizontal canal, mimicking head turn to the opposite side). In an awake, conscious patient, cold water in the right ear produces slow drift toward the right, followed by a fast corrective saccade to the opposite side (COWS: Cold Opposite, Warm Same for the fast phase). In a comatose patient with an INTACT brainstem, cortical saccadic mechanisms are lost; therefore, only the brainstem-mediated slow phase occurs: slow tonic conjugate deviation of both eyes TOWARD the cold-irrigated ear.
high_yield_pearl: Caloric testing: Conscious = COWS (fast saccades to Cold Opposite, Warm Same). Comatose with intact brainstem = slow tonic deviation TOWARD cold ear.

source: Content Q8: Superior Semicircular Canal Dehiscence
question: A 41-year-old woman presents with episodes of brief vertigo and oscillopsia triggered whenever she hears loud musical notes at church or when she blows her nose forcefully (Tullio phenomenon). She also complains of hearing her own voice unusually loud and echoing in her right ear (autophony) and can even hear her own footsteps and heartbeat. High-resolution temporal bone CT confirms an absent bony roof over the right superior semicircular canal. What is the physical mechanism causing these symptoms?

options.text: A 'third mobile window' in the otic capsule allowing acoustic sound pressure waves to directly deflect the cupula
An abnormal fistulous communication between the petrous internal carotid artery and the facial nerve canal
Excessive accumulation of dense calcium carbonate otoconia within the lateral horizontal semicircular canal
Infiltration and erosion of the round window membrane by chronic destructive cholesteatoma granulation tissue
Congenital absence of the stapedius muscle causing unprotected acoustic shock and excessive ossicular vibration

explanation: Superior canal dehiscence syndrome (SCDS) is caused by an abnormal opening (dehiscence) in the bony roof of the superior semicircular canal into the middle cranial fossa, creating an abnormal 'third mobile window' into the inner ear (in addition to the normal oval and round windows). Acoustic pressure waves or intracranial pressure changes (coughing, straining, Valsalva) dissipate across this dehiscent window, causing abnormal fluid displacement that deflects the cupula of the superior canal. This produces Tullio phenomenon (vertigo/oscillopsia induced by loud sounds), Hennebert sign (vertigo induced by pressure changes in EAC), and autophony.
high_yield_pearl: Superior canal dehiscence: 'Third mobile window' over superior canal -> Tullio phenomenon (sound-induced vertigo) & autophony (hearing heartbeat/voice loudly).

source: Content Q8: Perilymphatic Fistula
question: A 29-year-old scuba diver experiences sudden, severe right ear pain and popping while making an emergency rapid ascent from 90 feet. Immediately upon surfacing, he develops acute vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided hearing loss. In the emergency department, applying positive pneumatic pressure into his right external auditory canal with an otoscope elicits sudden vertigo and conjugate eye deviation (positive Hennebert sign). What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Acute bacterial labyrinthitis spreading from a pre-existing chronic otitis media
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo secondary to concussion-induced canalithiasis
Meniere's disease triggered by rapid changes in hydrostatic ambient pressure
Perilymphatic fistula caused by barotraumatic rupture of the round or oval window membrane
Air embolism occluding the anterior inferior cerebellar artery in the posterior fossa

explanation: A perilymphatic fistula is an abnormal leakage of perilymph from the inner ear into the middle ear, most frequently caused by a tear in the thin membrane of the round window or the annular ligament of the oval window. Common etiologies include barotrauma (scuba diving, blast injury, rapid flight descents), direct blunt head trauma, or vigorous straining. Clinical presentation is acute sensorineural hearing loss and episodic vertigo exacerbated by activities that increase middle ear pressure (pneumatic otoscopy: positive Hennebert sign) or intracranial pressure (coughing, sneezing, straining).
high_yield_pearl: Perilymphatic fistula: Tear in round or oval window (barotrauma/diving/straining) -> perilymph leak into middle ear -> pressure-induced vertigo (Hennebert sign).

source: Content Q3: Head Impulse Test (Halmagyi-Curthoys)
question: A physician evaluates a patient with acute persistent vertigo to determine whether a stroke or vestibular neuritis is present. The physician performs the horizontal Head Impulse Test (HIT): the patient fixates on the examiner's nose while the examiner rapidly turns the patient's head approximately 15 degrees to the right. The patient's eyes slide off the target to the right, followed immediately by a rapid, visible corrective catch-up saccade back to the examiner's nose. What does this positive catch-up saccade indicate?

options.text: An acute ischemic stroke confined to the left paramedian pontine reticular formation
Normal, completely intact bilateral peripheral vestibular ocular reflex pathways
A central internuclear ophthalmoplegia affecting the right medial longitudinal fasciculus
Complete destruction of the cerebellar vermis by a primary glioblastoma multiforme
A peripheral vestibular deficit in the right horizontal semicircular canal or vestibular nerve

explanation: The Head Impulse Test (HIT) is a critical component of the HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) used to differentiate peripheral from central acute vestibular syndromes. When the head is thrust rapidly toward a healthy ear, the intact VOR drives the eyes smoothly in the opposite direction, keeping fixation locked on the examiner's nose. If the peripheral VOR is damaged (e.g., right vestibular neuritis), turning the head to the right fails to rotate the eyes fast enough; the eyes move with the head off the target, requiring a visible, rapid 'catch-up saccade' back to the target. Thus, a refixation saccade toward one side indicates a PERIPHERAL vestibular lesion on that side.
high_yield_pearl: Positive Head Impulse Test: Catch-up saccade when thrusting head toward affected ear -> confirms PERIPHERAL vestibular loss (e.g. vestibular neuritis).

source: Lecture File 11 Slide 21 & Content Q3: Motion Sickness Neurobiology
question: A 24-year-old medical student feels nauseated, cold, pale, and diaphoretic while reading lecture notes in the back seat of a moving car on a winding mountain road. What sensory neurobiological mechanism produces motion sickness, and what is the first-line pharmacologic agent for its prevention?

options.text: Excessive activation of cochlear inner hair cells by engine noise; prevented with oral high-dose gabapentin
Sensory mismatch between visual inputs and vestibular otolith/canal signals; prevented with transdermal scopolamine
Direct bacterial enterotoxin release into the area postrema; prevented with oral broad-spectrum metronidazole
Acute endolymphatic hydrops driven by elevated sympathetic tone; prevented with intravenous furosemide
Ischemia of the vestibular nuclei due to vertebral artery kinking; prevented with therapeutic heparin anticoagulation

explanation: Motion sickness (kinetosis) results from a sensory conflict (mismatch) between different sensory modalities conveying spatial orientation: while the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals and otoliths) detects motion and acceleration, the visual system (reading stationary text inside the car) reports that the body is stationary. This conflicting sensory input is relayed from vestibular nuclei to the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema) and solitary tract, activating emetic and autonomic circuits. First-line prophylaxis is transdermal scopolamine (a centrally acting competitive muscarinic receptor antagonist) or H1-antihistamines (e.g., dimenhydrinate, meclizine).
high_yield_pearl: Motion sickness: Sensory conflict between vestibular (detecting motion) and visual (detecting stillness) inputs. Prophylaxis: Scopolamine (antimuscarinic).

source: Content Q14: Mal de Débarquement Syndrome
question: A 48-year-old woman returns from a 7-day Caribbean cruise. Upon stepping off the ship, she notes a continuous, distressing illusion of rocking, swaying, and bobbing, as if she were still on a ship deck at sea. Her hearing is normal, and brain MRI is unremarkable. Surprisingly, when she drives her car, her sensation of rocking completely disappears, only to return immediately once she stops. What condition does this patient have?

options.text: Vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia compressing the root exit zone of the vestibulocochlear nerve
Late-stage Meniere's disease with permanent distension of the endolymphatic duct
Acute bilateral vestibular schwannomas associated with neurofibromatosis type 2
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of both anterior and posterior semicircular canals
Mal de débarquement syndrome caused by maladaptive central vestibular neuroplastic adaptation

explanation: Mal de débarquement syndrome (MdDS) is a neurological disorder typically triggered by prolonged exposure to passive rhythmic motion (such as ocean travel on a cruise ship, flight, or train). While most travelers experience transient rocking for a few hours after disembarking ('land sickness'), patients with MdDS fail to readapt, suffering persistent illusions of self-motion (rocking, swaying, bobbing) that can last months to years. A unique, pathognomonic hallmark is that symptoms are temporarily relieved by re-exposure to passive motion (such as riding in an automobile).
high_yield_pearl: Mal de débarquement syndrome: Persistent rocking/swaying after cruise/travel; uniquely improves during passive vehicular motion.

source: Content Q6: Vestibular Schwannoma Surgical Complications
question: A 49-year-old man undergoes translabyrinthine surgical resection of a 3.5-cm vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle. Immediately postoperatively, he is noted to have complete flaccid paralysis of the ipsilateral upper and lower facial muscles, inability to close his eye, and loss of the corneal blink reflex on that side. Which anatomical nerve was damaged during the tumor removal?

options.text: Facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which runs intimately alongside the vestibulocochlear nerve in the internal acoustic meatus
Abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), which ascends through Dorello's canal
Trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), which enters the brainstem at the mid-pons level
Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI), which ascends through the foramen magnum
Glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), which traverses the pars nervosa of the jugular foramen

explanation: Cranial nerve VII (facial nerve) and cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) exit the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle and travel together into the internal acoustic meatus (IAM) through the petrous temporal bone. Vestibular schwannomas arise from the vestibular nerve within the IAM and expand into the CPA, intimately draping and compressing the facial nerve over the tumor capsule. Resection of large tumors carries a high surgical risk of stretching or transecting CN VII, leading to complete ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: Vestibular schwannoma surgery: CN VII and CN VIII travel together in the internal acoustic meatus -> high risk of CN VII injury & facial paralysis.

source: Content Q8: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus)
question: A 62-year-old man presents with severe burning pain deep inside his right ear, followed 3 days later by the appearance of painful, grouped vesicular eruptions on his right pinna and external auditory canal. He then develops acute flaccid paralysis of his entire right face (inability to furrow brow or close right eye), marked vertigo with nausea, and right-sided sensorineural hearing loss. Where was the latent pathogen located prior to reactivation?

options.text: Geniculate ganglion of cranial nerve VII with secondary involvement of adjacent cranial nerve VIII
Dorsal root ganglion of the second cervical spinal nerve
Inferior ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve within the jugular fossa
Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion situated anterior to the C2-C3 transverse processes
Trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion of cranial nerve V within Meckel's cave

explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes zoster oticus) is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII). The classic triad consists of: 1) Severe otalgia, 2) Vesicular lesions on the external ear (pinna, tragus, external auditory canal), and 3) Acute peripheral facial nerve paralysis (LMN CN VII palsy). Because CN VII and CN VIII travel intimately together within the facial canal and internal acoustic meatus, viral spread commonly causes cochleovestibular symptoms including sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and severe vertigo.
high_yield_pearl: Ramsay Hunt syndrome: VZV reactivation in geniculate ganglion (CN VII) -> ear vesicles + LMN facial palsy + vertigo/SNHL (CN VIII).

source: Case 3-4 & Content Q14: Multisensory Dizziness in Elderly
question: An 82-year-old woman is brought to clinic by her family because she feels progressively 'unsteady on her feet' and has fallen twice in the past 6 months. She describes her sensation not as true spinning vertigo, but as a vague, floating unsteadiness that worsens in dim lighting and when walking on uneven grassy surfaces. Neurological examination reveals bilateral mild high-frequency hearing loss, reduced vibration and position sense in both feet (distal peripheral neuropathy), and visual acuity of 20/70 due to cataracts. What is the diagnosis and primary management?

options.text: Multisensory dizziness of aging (presbyastasis); managed with physical therapy and vestibular balance rehabilitation
Meniere's disease; treated with bilateral surgical labyrinthectomy and vestibular neurectomy
Acute basilar artery thrombosis; treated with urgent catheter-directed intra-arterial thrombolysis
Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus; treated with urgent ventriculoperitoneal shunting
Bilateral acute labyrinthitis; treated with high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy

explanation: Multisensory dizziness (presbyastasis) is a common, multifactorial cause of chronic dysequilibrium in elderly individuals. Upright balance depends on the brain integrating inputs from three sensory systems: vestibular, visual, and somatosensory (proprioception). Age-related degeneration in two or more of these systems (e.g., loss of vestibular hair cells, cataractous visual decline, and diabetic or sensory peripheral neuropathy) leaves the patient unable to compensate when challenged by poor lighting or uneven surfaces. The condition is managed with fall-prevention measures, assistive devices, cataract extraction, and vestibular rehabilitation therapy.
high_yield_pearl: Presbyastasis: Multifactorial dysequilibrium in elderly from concurrent deficits in vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive systems. Managed with vestibular rehab.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 19-21 & Content Q8: Internal Capsule Somatotopy
question: A 64-year-old hypertensive woman has an ischemic stroke involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule. In addition to knowing that corticospinal fibers pass through this structure, the neurologist explains the precise somatotopic arrangement of descending motor fibers from anterior to posterior. In which sequence are body parts represented as the motor fibers travel through the posterior limb of the internal capsule?

options.text: Lower extremity in the genu, followed by the trunk, upper extremity, and face posteriorly
Face in the genu, followed by the upper extremity, trunk, and lower extremity in the posterior limb
Face, arm, trunk, and leg mixed randomly throughout the entire anterior limb
Trunk in the genu, followed by the face, lower extremity, and upper extremity posteriorly
Sensory fibers only in the posterior limb with all motor fibers passing through the anterior limb

explanation: The internal capsule demonstrates precise somatotopic organization: Corticobulbar fibers (which control the cranial nerve motor nuclei of the head and face) travel through the GENU. Immediately posterior to the genu, within the anterior half of the POSTERIOR LIMB, corticospinal fibers descend in a strict anterior-to-posterior somatotopic order: Upper Extremity (arm/hand) $\rightarrow$ Trunk $\rightarrow$ Lower Extremity (leg/foot). Farther posterior lie somatosensory thalamocortical fibers from VPL/VPM, followed by optic radiations in the retrolenticular part.
high_yield_pearl: Internal capsule motor somatotopy: Face/cranial nerves in GENU $\rightarrow$ Arm $\rightarrow$ Trunk $\rightarrow$ Leg in POSTERIOR LIMB.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 20 & Content Q8: Cerebral Peduncle Midbrain
question: On a transverse histological cross-section through the rostral midbrain, the cerebral peduncles (crus cerebri) form prominent ventral fiber bundles. Where within the crus cerebri do the descending corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts travel, and what fiber tracts flank them medially and laterally?

options.text: Middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri, flanked medially by frontopontine and laterally by parietotemporopontine fibers
Tegmentum between the red nucleus and substantia nigra, surrounded by reticular formation
Lateral one-fifth exclusively, flanked medially by the central tegmental tract and rubrospinal fibers
Medial one-fifth exclusively, flanked laterally by the spinothalamic tract and medial lemniscus
Periaqueductal gray region, flanked dorsally by the superior colliculi and trochlear nucleus

explanation: The crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) constitutes the massive ventral portion of the cerebral peduncles in the midbrain. The descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers occupy the middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri. They are flanked medially by frontopontine fibers (Arnold's bundle, medial 1/5) originating in the frontal lobe, and flanked laterally by parietopontine, temporopontine, and occipitopontine fibers (Türck's bundle, lateral 1/5). The substantia nigra lies directly dorsal to these descending peduncular tracts.
high_yield_pearl: Cerebral peduncle (midbrain): Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts occupy the MIDDLE 3/5 of the crus cerebri.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 24-25 & Content Q8: Pyramidal Decussation
question: At the cervicomedullary junction (caudal medulla), the descending corticospinal fibers undergo pyramidal decussation. What percentage of fibers cross the midline, where do the crossed fibers descend in the spinal cord, and what motor tasks do they control?

options.text: 10% cross to form the tectospinal tract in the anterior funiculus, coordinating autonomic respiration
50% cross to form the dorsal column tract, controlling proximal postural axial tone
All fibers remain uncrossed in the anterior funiculus to innervate ipsilateral intercostal muscles
100% cross to form the rubrospinal tract, controlling rhythmic stepping patterns during locomotion
85% to 90% cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus, controlling distal skilled limb movements

explanation: At the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, approximately 85% to 90% of corticospinal axons cross the midline to the contralateral side and descend in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord as the Lateral Corticospinal Tract. This tract terminates predominantly on lateral motor neuron pools in the cervical and lumbosacral enlargements to control distal, fractionated, skilled voluntary movements (especially fine finger and hand dexterity). The remaining 10% to 15% of fibers continue uncrossed as the Anterior Corticospinal Tract in the anterior funiculus, projecting bilaterally to medial motor neuron pools controlling axial and proximal girdle muscles for posture.
high_yield_pearl: Pyramidal decussation: 85-90% cross $\rightarrow$ Lateral Corticospinal Tract (lateral funiculus) $\rightarrow$ distal skilled movements. 10-15% uncrossed $\rightarrow$ Anterior tract (axial/posture).

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 30-32 & Content Q4: UMN vs. LMN Signs Comparison
question: A 56-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in his left arm and leg. Physical examination reveals spastic hypertonia, 4+ hyperactive biceps and patellar reflexes, ankle clonus, and a positive extensor plantar response (Babinski sign). In contrast, another patient in the clinic with a peripheral nerve transection exhibits flaccid weakness, areflexia, marked muscle wasting, and visible fasciculations. Which statement correctly categorizes and contrasts these findings?

options.text: Fasciculations and spasticity reflect UMN lesions, whereas hyperreflexia and Babinski sign reflect LMN lesions
Flaccidity and hyperreflexia reflect UMN lesions, whereas spasticity and muscle wasting reflect LMN lesions
Both sets of findings represent progressive stages of lower motor neuron degeneration without central involvement
Hyperreflexia, spasticity, and Babinski sign reflect UMN lesions, whereas flaccidity, fasciculations, and muscle atrophy reflect LMN lesions
Spasticity and fasciculations are pathognomonic of cerebellar hemisphere infarcts rather than motor pathway disease

explanation: Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesions (affecting the motor cortex or corticospinal tract) produce 'positive' signs of motor disinhibition: spasticity (velocity-dependent resistance to passive stretch), hyperactive deep tendon reflexes, sustained clonus, clasp-knife rigidity, and a positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response), with minimal disuse atrophy. Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesions (affecting the anterior horn cells, motor roots, or peripheral nerves) disrupt the final common pathway, producing 'negative' signs: flaccid paralysis/hypotonia, hyporeflexia or areflexia, severe neurogenic muscle wasting/atrophy, fasciculations (spontaneous visible motor unit twitches), and fibrillations on EMG.
high_yield_pearl: UMN lesion: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, +Babinski. LMN lesion: Flaccid paralysis, areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 29-31 & Content Q4: Mechanism of UMN Spasticity
question: Following an ischemic stroke affecting the primary motor cortex, a patient initially demonstrates flaccid paralysis that gradually evolves over several weeks into marked velocity-dependent spasticity, clasp-knife resistance, and hyperreflexia. What is the fundamental neurophysiological mechanism responsible for these 'positive' UMN symptoms?

options.text: Upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors across denervated skeletal muscle sarcolemma
Direct electrical ephaptic transmission between adjacent demyelinated peripheral axons
Autoimmune destruction of GABAergic interneurons within the dorsal root ganglion
Loss of descending cortical and reticulospinal inhibition, resulting in uninhibited hyperactivity of spinal reflex arcs
Selective degeneration of primary group Ia sensory afferent fibers within the muscle spindles

explanation: In the intact nervous system, descending projections from the motor cortex and dorsal reticulospinal tracts exert tonic, continuous inhibitory control over spinal segmental reflex arcs (via GABAergic and glycinergic spinal interneurons like Renshaw cells). Following a chronic UMN lesion, this descending inhibitory control is lost. As spinal circuits undergo synaptic remodeling and hypersensitivity, segmental stretch reflexes become uninhibited and hyperactive, causing hyperreflexia, clonus, and velocity-dependent spasticity (resistance increases as passive stretching velocity increases).
high_yield_pearl: UMN spasticity/hyperreflexia mechanism: Loss of descending inhibitory control from cortex/reticulospinal tracts $\rightarrow$ uninhibited spinal stretch reflexes.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 11, 32 & Content Q4: Fasciculations vs. Fibrillations
question: A 48-year-old mechanic with a traumatic brachial plexus injury develops profound muscle weakness in his right shoulder and arm. On examination, the physician observes fine, spontaneous, involuntary flickering twitches beneath the skin of the deltoid and biceps muscles. Needle electromyography (EMG) confirms both fasciculation potentials and fibrillation potentials. How do fasciculations and fibrillations differ in their cellular origins and clinical visibility?

options.text: Fasciculations originate in the primary motor cortex; fibrillations originate in the sensory dorsal root ganglion
Fasciculations indicate acute upper motor neuron injury; fibrillations indicate chronic cerebellar Purkinje cell loss
Both represent synchronized action potentials in the posterior columns with no relationship to lower motor neurons
Fasciculations are spontaneous discharges of an entire motor unit visible to the naked eye; fibrillations are contractions of single muscle fibers visible only on EMG
Fibrillations are visible to the naked eye through the skin; fasciculations are detectable only on microscopic muscle biopsy

explanation: Fasciculations and fibrillations are cardinal electrophysiological hallmarks of lower motor neuron denervation. A fasciculation is the spontaneous, involuntary firing of a sick or dying anterior horn cell or its axon, which causes synchronous contraction of all muscle fibers in that entire motor unit; because an entire motor unit contracts, fasciculations are visible beneath the skin to the naked eye. In contrast, a fibrillation potential is the spontaneous, rhythmic action potential of a single, denervated muscle fiber (due to denervation acetylcholine hypersensitivity); single muscle fiber contractions generate too little force to be visible through the skin and can be detected only as electrical potentials on needle EMG.
high_yield_pearl: Fasciculations = whole motor unit discharge, visible to naked eye. Fibrillations = single denervated muscle fiber contraction, seen only on EMG.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 30, 32 & Content Q7: Babinski Reflex Physiology
question: When a clinician strokes the lateral plantar surface of a normal adult foot from the heel forward to the ball of the foot with a blunt probe, the normal response is plantar flexion (curling downward) of all toes. However, in a patient with a spinal cord compression, the great toe extends upward (dorsiflexes) and the other toes fan outward (positive Babinski sign). What is the physiological basis of this extensor plantar response?

options.text: Overactivation of the Golgi tendon organ reflex within the gastrocnemius tendon
Acute rupture of the flexor digitorum brevis tendon along the plantar aponeurosis
Irritation of the cutaneous mechanoreceptors supplied by the saphenous nerve
Sympathetic vasoconstriction of the dorsal digital arteries causing muscle ischemia
Loss of descending corticospinal suppression unmasks a primitive spinal flexion withdrawal reflex

explanation: The Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) is a pathognomonic indicator of corticospinal (UMN) tract damage. In healthy adults, intact descending corticospinal tracts tonically suppress primitive cutaneous withdrawal reflexes, ensuring that plantar stimulation elicits toe flexion. When corticospinal fibers are damaged, this central suppression is abolished, unmasking the primitive spinal nociceptive flexion reflex (extensor hallucis longus activation $\rightarrow$ great toe dorsiflexion and fanning of lesser toes). The Babinski reflex is physiologically normal in neonates and infants up to 12-24 months of age because corticospinal myelination is not yet complete.
high_yield_pearl: Babinski sign (+ extensor plantar response): Corticospinal (UMN) lesion unmasks primitive flexion withdrawal reflex $\rightarrow$ great toe dorsiflexes, toes fan out. Normal in infants <2yo.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 44-48 & Content Q8: Corticobulbar Tract Anatomy
question: The corticobulbar (corticonuclear) tract conveys voluntary motor commands from the cerebral cortex to the motor cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem. What is the precise origin, internal capsule trajectory, and termination of these upper motor neurons?

options.text: Originates in the postcentral gyrus, descends through the retrolenticular capsule, and terminates in the lateral geniculate body
Originates in the supplementary motor area, descends through the anterior limb of the internal capsule, and terminates in the substantia nigra
Originates in the face region of the precentral gyrus, descends through the genu of the internal capsule, and terminates on brainstem motor cranial nerve nuclei
Originates in the frontal eye fields, descends through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, and terminates in the cuneate nucleus
Originates in the cerebellar vermis, descends through the superior cerebellar peduncle, and terminates in the red nucleus

explanation: The corticobulbar tract consists of upper motor neurons that arise from the ventral 'face and tongue' representation of the primary motor cortex (inferior precentral gyrus) and adjacent premotor cortex. These fibers converge through the corona radiata to pass specifically through the GENU of the internal capsule (flanked by frontopontine fibers in the anterior limb and corticospinal fibers in the posterior limb). They descend into the brainstem tegmentum to synapse upon motor nuclei of cranial nerves: CN V (mastication), CN VII (facial expression), CN IX/X (nucleus ambiguus: swallowing/speech), CN XI (sternocleidomastoid/trapezius), and CN XII (tongue).
high_yield_pearl: Corticobulbar tract: Precentral gyrus face area $\rightarrow$ GENU of internal capsule $\rightarrow$ motor cranial nerve nuclei in brainstem.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 48, 55 & Content Q8, 9: Bilateral Corticobulbar Innervation
question: A 72-year-old man suffers a severe ischemic stroke in the left precentral gyrus. On neurological examination, jaw movements and chewing are completely symmetrical, swallowing is normal, and both sides of the soft palate elevate symmetrically on phonation. Which neuroanatomical principle explains why mastication and palatal function remain intact despite a unilateral motor cortex destruction?

options.text: The left motor cortex sends inhibitory fibers, so a stroke leads to spastic muscle contraction
Mastication and deglutition are driven solely by cerebellar purkinje cell pacemakers
The motor nucleus of CN V and the nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X) receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation
The corticobulbar tract completely decussates in the midbrain to provide exclusive contralateral supply
These cranial nerve motor nuclei are entirely autonomous and receive no cortical projections

explanation: Most motor cranial nerve nuclei receive BILATERAL corticobulbar projections from both cerebral hemispheres. These include: the motor nucleus of CN V (muscles of mastication), the nucleus ambiguus (CN IX and X, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles for swallowing and vocal cords), and the upper face subnucleus of CN VII. Therefore, a unilateral UMN lesion (such as a stroke in one motor cortex or internal capsule) produces NO significant weakness in the jaw, palate, or vocal cords, because the intact contralateral hemisphere continues to provide motor drive to both sides of these nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: Bilateral corticobulbar innervation: CN V (mastication), CN IX/X (nucleus ambiguus, palate/swallow) $\rightarrow$ unilateral UMN stroke causes NO deficit.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 49-54 & Content Q10: CN VII UMN vs. LMN Lesion (Forehead Sparing)
question: A 67-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with acute weakness of the right side of his face. On examination, when asked to smile, the right corner of his mouth droops and he cannot puff out his right cheek. However, when asked to raise his eyebrows and wrinkle his forehead, both sides of his forehead wrinkle symmetrically, and he can close both eyes tightly. Where is the lesion located, and why is his upper face spared?

options.text: Right geniculate ganglion within the temporal bone; the upper facial branch recovers faster from viral inflammation
Right facial motor nucleus in the caudal pons (LMN lesion); the frontalis muscle is protected by collateral motor axons from CN VI
Left oculomotor nucleus in the rostral midbrain; levator palpebrae superioris compensates for frontalis paralysis
Right facial nerve in the stylomastoid foramen (LMN lesion); the forehead muscles are innervated by the trigeminal nerve
Left motor cortex or corticobulbar tract (UMN lesion); the upper face motor nucleus of CN VII receives bilateral corticobulbar input

explanation: The facial motor nucleus (CN VII) in the caudal pons is anatomically divided into two subnuclei: 1) The dorsal subnucleus, which innervates muscles of the UPPER face (frontalis and orbicularis oculi), receives BILATERAL corticobulbar innervation. 2) The ventral subnucleus, which innervates muscles of the LOWER face, receives ONLY CONTRALATERAL corticobulbar innervation. In a unilateral UMN lesion (e.g., left MCA stroke or internal capsule infarct), the left upper face subnucleus still receives input from the intact right hemisphere, sparing the right forehead. In contrast, an LMN lesion (Bell's palsy or CN VII nucleus lesion) destroys the final common pathway, causing complete flaccid paralysis of the entire ipsilateral face (both upper forehead and lower mouth).
high_yield_pearl: CN VII UMN lesion (stroke): Contralateral lower face droops, FOREHEAD SPARED (bilateral UMN input). CN VII LMN lesion (Bell's palsy): ENTIRE ipsilateral face paralyzed.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 43, 58 & Content Q10: CN XII Tongue Deviation (UMN vs. LMN)
question: Two patients present with tongue deviation on protrusion. Patient A has an ischemic stroke of the right precentral gyrus (UMN lesion). Patient B has a traumatic transection of the right hypoglossal nerve in the neck (LMN lesion). To which side does the tongue deviate in each patient, and what associated findings differentiate them?

options.text: Patient A's tongue deviates to the left (contralateral) without atrophy; Patient B's tongue deviates to the right (ipsilateral) with atrophy and fasciculations
Patient A's tongue remains strictly midline; Patient B's tongue deviates bilaterally with loss of sensation
Both patients' tongues deviate to the right with prominent fasciculations and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds
Both patients' tongues deviate to the left with bilateral hyperreflexia of the masseter stretch reflex
Patient A's tongue deviates to the right with fasciculations; Patient B's tongue deviates to the left without atrophy

explanation: The genioglossus muscle protrudes the tongue by pushing it forward and toward the opposite (contralateral) side. In normal health, both genioglossi push equally, keeping the tongue in the midline. The hypoglossal motor nucleus receives predominantly contralateral corticobulbar input. In Patient A (UMN lesion of right motor cortex): the left genioglossus is paretic; when the patient protrudes the tongue, the intact right genioglossus pushes unopposed, causing the tongue to deviate to the CONTRALATERAL (LEFT) side, without muscle wasting. In Patient B (LMN lesion of right CN XII): the right genioglossus is paralyzed and atrophic; the intact left genioglossus pushes unopposed, causing the tongue to deviate toward the IPSILATERAL (RIGHT / damaged) side, with marked muscle atrophy and fasciculations ('licks the lesion').
high_yield_pearl: Hypoglossal lesion: LMN (CN XII) = deviates IPSILATERAL (toward lesion) with atrophy/fasciculations. UMN (cortex/capsule) = deviates CONTRALATERAL (away from lesion) without atrophy.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 42-43 & Content Q9: CN XI (Accessory Nerve) Examination
question: A 24-year-old man undergoes lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. Postoperatively, he has difficulty elevating his right arm above the horizontal plane and complains of a drooping right shoulder. When asked to turn his head forcefully to the left against resistance, the contraction of his right sternocleidomastoid muscle is markedly weakened. Which cranial nerve was injured, and what is its peripheral course?

options.text: Hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII), which crosses the carotid triangle superficial to the hyoglossus muscle
Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI), which emerges from cervical cord segments C1-C5 and traverses the posterior triangle of the neck
Phrenic nerve, which descends along the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle in the neck
Glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), which passes through the jugular foramen and courses around the stylopharyngeus
Ansa cervicalis, which loops around the internal jugular vein to supply the infrahyoid strap muscles

explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from lower motor neurons located in the anterior horn of cervical spinal cord segments C1 through C5. Its rootlets ascend through the foramen magnum, join the cranial rootlets briefly, exit the skull via the jugular foramen, and course superficial to the levator scapulae in the posterior triangle of the neck. It innervates the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and trapezius muscles. Contraction of the right SCM turns the head to the CONTRALATERAL (left) side. The trapezius elevates the shoulder. Its superficial location in the posterior cervical triangle makes CN XI vulnerable to injury during lymph node biopsies, resulting in shoulder drop, winging of the scapula, and impaired contralateral head rotation.
high_yield_pearl: CN XI (Accessory nerve): Innervates SCM (turns head to opposite side) & Trapezius (elevates shoulder). Vulnerable in posterior triangle of neck.

source: Content Q11 & Case 3: Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine)
question: A 63-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension collapses at work. Examination reveals: 1) Flaccid paralysis and fasciculations of the right half of his tongue, with deviation to the right on protrusion; 2) Spastic hemiplegia of his left arm and leg with hyperreflexia and a positive left Babinski sign; 3) Loss of vibration and proprioception (joint position sense) in his left arm and leg with spared pain and temperature sensation. Occlusion of which artery caused this brainstem stroke?

options.text: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA), causing paramedian midbrain infarction
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), causing lateral medullary syndrome
Superior cerebellar artery (SCA), causing dorsal midbrain syndrome
Anterior spinal artery or paramedian branches of the vertebral artery, causing medial medullary syndrome
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), causing lateral pontine syndrome

explanation: Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine syndrome) results from infarction of the medial medulla due to occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) or vertebral artery paramedian branches. The ischemic territory damages three key longitudinal structures: 1) Hypoglossal nerve rootlets (CN XII) $\rightarrow$ ipsilateral LMN tongue weakness, atrophy, and deviation to the right. 2) Corticospinal tract in the medullary pyramid (prior to decussation) $\rightarrow$ contralateral spastic hemiplegia (left hemiparesis, +Babinski). 3) Medial lemniscus $\rightarrow$ contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration sense (left side). The spinothalamic tract is lateral and spared, preserving pain and temperature.
high_yield_pearl: Medial medullary syndrome (ASA occlusion): Ipsilateral tongue deviation (CN XII) + Contralateral spastic hemiplegia (pyramid) + Contralateral loss of proprioception/vibration (medial lemniscus).

source: Content Q11: Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenberg)
question: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden vertigo, nausea, vomiting, intractable hiccups, and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) with a hoarse voice. Examination shows: loss of the gag reflex on the right, deviation of the uvula to the left, right Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), right-sided limb ataxia with dysmetria, loss of pain and temperature over the right side of the face, and loss of pain and temperature over the left arm, trunk, and leg. Muscle strength in all four limbs is completely normal (5/5). Occlusion of which vessel accounts for this stroke?

options.text: Labyrinthine artery, causing isolated cochleovestibular ischemia with peripheral deafness and nystagmus
Anterior spinal artery (ASA), causing medial medullary syndrome with crossed hemiplegia and CN XII palsy
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), causing lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome)
Middle cerebral artery (MCA), causing contralateral hemiplegia and sensory loss across the upper body
Basilar artery perforating branches, causing paramedian caudal pontine infarction and hemiparesis

explanation: Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. Key involved structures include: 1) Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X) $\rightarrow$ dysphagia, hoarseness, absent right gag reflex, uvula deviates to the left (opposite side). 2) Vestibular nuclei $\rightarrow$ severe vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting. 3) Inferior cerebellar peduncle $\rightarrow$ ipsilateral limb ataxia. 4) Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract $\rightarrow$ loss of facial pain and temperature on the IPSILATERAL (right) side. 5) Spinothalamic tract $\rightarrow$ loss of body pain and temperature on the CONTRALATERAL (left) side ('crossed' sensory loss). 6) Descending sympathetic tract $\rightarrow$ ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Crucially, the motor pyramid is in the medial medulla and is spared; motor strength is normal.
high_yield_pearl: Lateral medullary syndrome (PICA stroke): Nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia/hoarseness) + Vertigo + Ipsilateral face / Contralateral body pain/temp loss + Horner syndrome. NO MOTOR WEAKNESS.

source: Content Q11: Weber Syndrome (Paramedian Midbrain)
question: A 70-year-old diabetic man develops sudden diplopia and left-sided hemiplegia. Examination reveals that his right eye is turned 'down and out', with severe ptosis of the right upper eyelid and a widely dilated right pupil that is non-reactive to light. The left arm and left leg demonstrate 1/5 muscle strength with spastic hypertonia, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes, and an extensor plantar response. Where is the infarct located, and which two anatomical structures are involved?

options.text: Dorsal rostral midbrain (Parinaud syndrome), involving the pretectal area and posterior commissure
Caudal pontine tegmentum (Foville syndrome), involving the abducens nucleus and facial motor nucleus
Ventral medial medulla (Dejerine syndrome), involving the pyramid and hypoglossal nerve fibers
Ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome), involving the fascicles of CN III and the corticospinal tract in the crus cerebri
Lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome), involving the spinothalamic tract and inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia) is a classical vascular brainstem syndrome caused by occlusion of the paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) or basilar bifurcation, infarcting the ventral midbrain. The lesion damages: 1) Oculomotor nerve (CN III) fascicles exiting through the tegmentum $\rightarrow$ ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, 'down and out' eye position, non-reactive mydriasis). 2) Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts descending in the middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle) $\rightarrow$ contralateral spastic hemiplegia (left hemiparesis with UMN signs).
high_yield_pearl: Weber syndrome (ventral midbrain, PCA branch): Ipsilateral CN III palsy (down & out, blown pupil) + Contralateral spastic hemiplegia (cerebral peduncle).

source: Content Q11: Millard-Gubler Syndrome (Caudal Pons)
question: A 61-year-old man has a stroke in the caudal ventral pons. On examination, he is unable to abduct his right eye past the midline on horizontal gaze (right internal strabismus). He has complete flaccid paralysis of the entire right side of his face, including inability to wrinkle his right forehead or close his right eye. In addition, he has spastic hemiparesis and hyperreflexia of his left arm and left leg. Which three structures are damaged in this Millard-Gubler syndrome?

options.text: Abducens nerve (CN VI), facial nerve (CN VII), and the corticospinal tract in the ventral caudal pons
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and dorsal column nuclei
Oculomotor nerve (CN III), red nucleus, and the medial lemniscus in the dorsal tegmentum
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), medial longitudinal fasciculus, and the sympathetic tract
Trochlear nerve (CN IV), trigeminal nerve (CN V), and the spinothalamic tract in the midbrain

explanation: Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral caudal pontine syndrome) is typically caused by occlusion of circumferential branches of the basilar artery or anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA). The lesion damages three structures passing through the ventral caudal pons: 1) Abducens nerve (CN VI) fibers $\rightarrow$ ipsilateral lateral rectus paralysis (inability to abduct the right eye). 2) Facial nerve (CN VII) fibers $\rightarrow$ complete ipsilateral peripheral (LMN) facial paralysis involving both forehead and lower mouth. 3) Uncrossed corticospinal tract fibers $\rightarrow$ contralateral spastic hemiplegia of the left arm and leg.
high_yield_pearl: Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral caudal pons): Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + Ipsilateral CN VII palsy (entire face) + Contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal).

source: Content Q11: Foville Syndrome (Dorsal Caudal Pons)
question: A patient presents with acute horizontal conjugate gaze paralysis: when asked to look to the right, neither eye can move past the midline to the right, although leftward horizontal gaze is intact. In addition, the patient exhibits complete right-sided peripheral facial paralysis (involving upper and lower face) and left spastic hemiparesis. What additional structure is involved in this Foville syndrome compared to Millard-Gubler?

options.text: Trochlear nucleus, causing vertical diplopia and compensatory head tilting
Superior colliculus, causing vertical upward gaze paralysis and lid retraction
Medial longitudinal fasciculus alone, causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia on contralateral gaze
Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) or abducens nucleus, causing conjugate lateral gaze palsy toward the lesion
Frontal eye field in the contralateral cerebral cortex, causing eyes to look toward the hemiplegia

explanation: Foville syndrome is a dorsal caudal pontine tegmental syndrome. While Millard-Gubler involves the exiting nerve root of CN VI (causing isolated ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy), Foville syndrome involves the abducens nucleus itself or the adjacent Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF). Because the abducens nucleus contains internuclear neurons that project to the contralateral medial rectus via the MLF, a nuclear/PPRF lesion paralyzes CONJUGATE horizontal gaze toward the side of the lesion (conjugate lateral gaze palsy). Associated damage to the adjacent CN VII fascicle produces ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy, and damage to the underlying corticospinal tract produces contralateral hemiparesis.
high_yield_pearl: Foville syndrome: Caudal pontine tegmentum involving PPRF/CN VI nucleus + CN VII + corticospinal $\rightarrow$ Conjugate gaze palsy toward lesion + facial palsy + hemiplegia.

source: Content Q11: Raymond Syndrome
question: A 65-year-old woman with small-vessel vascular disease presents with acute double vision and left-sided body weakness. Physical examination reveals an isolated inability to abduct the right eye on right lateral gaze, with normal vertical eye movements and normal adduction of both eyes. The facial muscles are completely symmetrical and normal. Muscle testing shows spastic weakness of the left arm and leg with an upgoing toe. Which structures are infarcted in this Raymond syndrome?

options.text: Cervical spinal cord involving the anterior horn cells and dorsal columns
Lateral medulla involving the inferior olivary nucleus and solitary tract
Ventral midbrain involving CN III fascicles and the substantia nigra
Dorsal rostral pons involving the medial lemniscus and superior cerebellar peduncle
Ventral medial pons involving ipsilateral CN VI fascicles and the corticospinal tract, with sparing of CN VII

explanation: Raymond syndrome is a ventral medial caudal pontine syndrome. It is caused by an infarct of the paramedian branches of the basilar artery that damages the exiting fascicles of the abducens nerve (CN VI) and the descending corticospinal tract, but is small and medial enough to spare the more laterally positioned facial nerve (CN VII) fibers. Consequently, it presents with an ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (inability to abduct the ipsilateral eye) and contralateral hemiparesis, but WITHOUT facial paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: Raymond syndrome (ventral medial pons): Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + Contralateral hemiparesis (spares CN VII).

source: Content Q11: Claude vs. Benedikt Syndrome
question: Two patients present with midbrain infarctions. Both have an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. Patient 1 additionally exhibits contralateral cerebellar ataxia and intention tremor. Patient 2 exhibits contralateral involuntary, slow, writhing movements (choreoathetosis) and coarse resting tremor in addition to ataxia. Which deep midbrain nuclei are involved in Claude syndrome (Patient 1) versus Benedikt syndrome (Patient 2)?

options.text: Claude involves CN III and the pyramidal tract; Benedikt involves CN III and the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Claude involves CN III and the locus coeruleus; Benedikt involves CN III and the periaqueductal gray
Claude involves CN III and the red nucleus; Benedikt involves CN III, red nucleus, and the substantia nigra
Claude involves CN III and the superior colliculus; Benedikt involves CN III and the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Claude involves CN III and the abducens nucleus; Benedikt involves CN III and the vestibular nuclei

explanation: Claude and Benedikt syndromes are midbrain tegmental syndromes affecting CN III fascicles plus adjacent midbrain structures. In Claude syndrome, the lesion involves CN III fascicles plus the red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle, producing ipsilateral CN III palsy combined with contralateral cerebellar ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremor. In Benedikt syndrome (paramedian midbrain syndrome), the infarct extends deeper and more ventrally to involve CN III fascicles, the red nucleus, and the substantia nigra (and striatonigral fibers), producing ipsilateral CN III palsy combined with contralateral ataxia PLUS hyperkinetic movement disorders (choreoathetosis, resting tremor, and rigidity).
high_yield_pearl: Midbrain syndromes: Weber = CN III + Crus cerebri (hemiplegia). Claude = CN III + Red nucleus (ataxia). Benedikt = CN III + Red nucleus + Substantia nigra (chorea/athetosis).

source: Content Q12: Pseudobulbar vs. Bulbar Palsy
question: A 72-year-old woman with extensive bilateral subcortical lacunar strokes presents with progressive slurred speech and swallowing difficulty. Examination reveals a spastic, contracted tongue that cannot be protruded quickly, an exaggerated hyperactive jaw jerk reflex, a hyperactive gag reflex, and episodes of uncontrollable, involuntary crying when greeted. In contrast, a patient with ALS and bulbar palsy exhibits a flaccid, severely wasted tongue with prominent fasciculations and an absent gag reflex. What is the fundamental anatomical distinction between pseudobulbar palsy and bulbar palsy?

options.text: Pseudobulbar palsy is a unilateral cortical hemisphere deficit; bulbar palsy requires total transection of the midbrain tectum
Pseudobulbar palsy is confined to the vagus nerve alone; bulbar palsy affects only the trigeminal and abducens nerves
Pseudobulbar palsy is caused by bilateral UMN lesions of the corticobulbar tracts; bulbar palsy is caused by LMN lesions of the lower cranial nerve nuclei
Pseudobulbar palsy is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction; bulbar palsy is caused by cerebellar vermis atrophy
Pseudobulbar palsy involves primary degeneration of muscle fibers; bulbar palsy is caused by sensory peripheral polyneuropathy

explanation: Bulbar palsy is a Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) disorder caused by bilateral damage to the lower cranial nerve motor nuclei (CN IX, X, XI, XII) in the medulla ('the bulb') or their peripheral nerves. Findings are flaccid: wasted atrophic tongue with fasciculations, absent gag reflex, dysphagia, and nasal dysarthria. Pseudobulbar palsy is an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) disorder caused by bilateral disruption of the descending corticobulbar tracts (e.g., bilateral lacunar strokes, MS, or ALS). Findings are spastic: a spastic, stiff tongue without wasting, hyperactive jaw jerk reflex (masseter reflex), hyperactive gag reflex, spastic dysarthria ('Donald Duck' voice), and pseudobulbar affect (pathological emotional lability: inappropriate laughter or crying unlinked to mood).
high_yield_pearl: Pseudobulbar palsy = Bilateral UMN corticobulbar lesion (spastic tongue, hyperactive jaw jerk, emotional lability). Bulbar palsy = Bilateral LMN lesion (atrophic tongue, fasciculations, absent gag).

source: Content Q8: Pure Motor Lacunar Stroke
question: A 59-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled hypertension awakens with complete paralysis of the left side of his body. Examination demonstrates 0/5 strength in the left lower face, left arm, and left leg, with hyperreflexia and an upgoing left toe. Sensations of touch, pinprick, vibration, and joint position are completely normal and symmetrical in all four limbs. He has no visual field defects, no dysarthria, and no hemineglect. What is the underlying vascular pathology and precise neuroanatomical localization?

options.text: Rupture of a berry aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery bifurcation with subarachnoid hemorrhage
Embolic occlusion of the main trunk of the anterior cerebral artery causing cortical paracentral lobule infarction
Atherosclerotic stenosis of the basilar artery compromising circumferential pontine branches
Lipohyalinosis and microatheroma of lenticulostriate arteries occluding the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery in the anterior median fissure of the cervical spinal cord

explanation: Pure Motor Stroke (Pure Motor Hemiparesis) is the most common lacunar stroke syndrome (accounting for ~50% of lacunar infarcts). It is caused by lipohyalinosis, microatheroma, or microthrombi involving the small, penetrating lenticulostriate arteries (branches of the MCA). The resulting small (<1.5 cm) infarct damages descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers tightly packed within the posterior limb of the internal capsule (or ventral basilar pons). Because sensory pathways (VPL/thalamus) and cortical association areas are spared, the patient exhibits dense contralateral hemiparesis affecting face, arm, and leg equally WITHOUT sensory loss, visual field cuts, aphasia, or neglect.
high_yield_pearl: Pure motor stroke: Hypertensive lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate arteries $\rightarrow$ lacunar infarct in posterior limb of internal capsule $\rightarrow$ dense hemiparesis WITHOUT sensory loss or aphasia.

source: Content Q5: Spinal Shock Physiology
question: A 22-year-old motorcyclist sustains a traumatic fracture-dislocation of the T4 vertebra with complete anatomical transection of the spinal cord. In the emergency department 2 hours after the injury, examination below T4 reveals complete flaccid paralysis of both legs, total absence of patellar and Achilles reflexes (0/4), an absent bulbocavernosus reflex, and a flaccid, atonic urinary bladder. Four weeks later, the patient's legs become hypertonic and spastic, with brisk 4+ tendon reflexes, sustained ankle clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. What phenomenon explains the initial temporary absence of reflexes?

options.text: Irreversible rupture of the anterior spinal artery causing anterior horn cell apoptosis
Spinal shock characterized by sudden loss of descending supraspinal tonic facilitation to spinal reflex arcs
Transient autoimmune blockade of voltage-gated potassium channels along peripheral nerves
Acute hypocalcemic tetany secondary to traumatic parathyroid gland devascularization
Permanent ischemic necrosis of all lower motor neuron cell bodies in the lumbosacral cord

explanation: Spinal shock is the transient, temporary physiological cessation of all spinal cord function below the level of an acute spinal cord injury. Although chronic UMN lesions cause hyperreflexia and spasticity, acute transection immediately deprives spinal reflex arcs of tonic descending supraspinal facilitation (from corticospinal and reticulospinal tracts). During this initial phase (lasting days to several weeks), the isolated spinal cord segments are quiescent: muscles are flaccid, all somatic and autonomic deep tendon and visceral reflexes are absent (areflexia, atonic bladder, loss of bulbocavernosus reflex), and sympathectomy causes vasodilation. As spinal circuits undergo denervation supersensitivity and collateral sprouting over weeks, the classic UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski) emerge.
high_yield_pearl: Spinal shock: Acute phase after cord injury $\rightarrow$ flaccidity and areflexia due to sudden loss of descending facilitation; evolves weeks later into spasticity & hyperreflexia.

source: Case 5 & Content Q13: Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Spinal Hemisection)
question: A 20-year-old man is stabbed in the back outside a nightclub. Neurological exam reveals a functional hemisection of the left thoracic spinal cord at the T8 level (Brown-Séquard syndrome). Which constellation of neurological deficits will be observed below the T8 level?
