options.text: Bilateral flaccid paralysis of both legs with selective sparing of proprioception and light touch
Ipsilateral spastic paresis, ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature
Ipsilateral loss of pain/temperature sensation with complete preservation of voluntary motor power bilaterally
Contralateral spastic paresis, contralateral loss of vibration, and ipsilateral loss of pain/temperature
Bilateral loss of motor function and bilateral loss of all sensory modalities in both lower extremities

explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection (damage to one lateral half) of the spinal cord. The anatomical tracts involved and their crossing patterns dictate the clinical picture below the lesion: 1) Lateral Corticospinal Tract (crossed in medulla) $\rightarrow$ IPSILATERAL spastic hemiparesis/paralysis below the lesion (+Babinski). 2) Dorsal Columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus, uncrossed in cord) $\rightarrow$ IPSILATERAL loss of vibration, joint position sense (proprioception), and fine touch below the lesion. 3) Lateral Spinothalamic Tract (crossed in spinal cord 1-2 segments above entry via anterior white commissure) $\rightarrow$ CONTRALATERAL loss of pain and temperature sensation starting 1 to 2 segments below the level of the lesion. At the level of the lesion, damage to anterior horn cells causes ipsilateral LMN flaccid weakness.
high_yield_pearl: Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection): Ipsilateral spastic paresis (corticospinal) + Ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception (dorsal column) + Contralateral loss of pain/temp (spinothalamic).

source: Content Q13: Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome
question: A 68-year-old man undergoes surgical repair of a descending thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Postoperatively, he has complete flaccid paraplegia of both lower extremities and total loss of pain and temperature sensation below the T10 dermatome, along with acute urinary retention. Remarkably, testing of vibration sense with a 128 Hz tuning fork and joint position sense in both great toes is completely normal and intact. Which vascular territory is infarcted, and why are vibration and proprioception spared?

options.text: Anterior spinal artery territory infarcted; posterior columns are spared because they are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries
Deep cervical artery territory infarcted; corticospinal tracts are spared due to retrograde anterior radicular filling
Great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz infarcted; dorsal roots are spared because they lack oxidative metabolic demands
Sulcocommissural artery territory infarcted; spinothalamic tracts are spared because they receive direct venous perfusion
Posterior spinal artery territory infarcted; anterior horns are spared by collateral flow from the internal vertebral plexus

explanation: The spinal cord receives its blood supply from a single Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA) supplying the anterior two-thirds of the cord, and paired Posterior Spinal Arteries (PSAs) supplying the posterior one-third. The artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radicular artery, typically arising from a left intercostal artery between T9-T12) provides crucial supply to the lumbosacral ASA. Interruption during aortic surgery causes Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome: infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the cord destroys the lateral corticospinal tracts (bilateral paraplegia), anterior horn cells (areflexia), and lateral spinothalamic tracts (bilateral loss of pain and temperature). In contrast, the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis) lie in the posterior third and are perfused by the intact posterior spinal arteries, completely preserving vibration, proprioception, and light touch.
high_yield_pearl: Anterior spinal artery syndrome: Bilateral paralysis (corticospinal) + Bilateral loss of pain/temp (spinothalamic). DORSAL COLUMNS SPARED (vibration/proprioception intact).

source: Content Q13: Central Cord Syndrome (Syringomyelia / Hyperextension)
question: A 72-year-old man with cervical spinal stenosis sustains a hyperextension injury to his neck in a motor vehicle collision. On examination, he has marked, severe flaccid weakness (1/5) and wasting in his hands and forearms, whereas muscle strength in his hips, knees, and ankles is remarkably preserved (4/5). He also exhibits bilateral 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature across his shoulders and upper arms. What is the diagnosis, and why are his arms weaker than his legs?

options.text: Guillain-Barré syndrome; peripheral motor nerves to the upper extremity possess higher myelin lipid density
Central cord syndrome; cervical corticospinal fibers controlling the arms lie medially in the lateral corticospinal tract
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; Betz cells controlling the hands have higher mitochondrial calcium sensitivity
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis; the lumbar enlargement receives primary perfusion from the cervical plexus
Brown-Séquard syndrome; lumbosacral fibers cross the anterior white commissure before cervical fibers

explanation: Central Cord Syndrome is the most common incomplete spinal cord injury, typically occurring in elderly patients with pre-existing cervical spondylosis following neck hyperextension (or from an expanding syringomyelia). Because the center of the cervical cord is damaged, two findings occur: 1) Disruption of decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure $\rightarrow$ bilateral 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature across the shoulders and arms. 2) Damage to the medial aspect of the lateral corticospinal tracts. In the lateral corticospinal tract, fibers are laminated somatotopically: cervical fibers (arm/hand) lie medially, while lumbosacral fibers (leg/foot) lie laterally on the periphery. Therefore, a central lesion injures medial cervical fibers preferentially, causing profound weakness in the upper extremities while relatively sparing the lower extremities ('arms weaker than legs').
high_yield_pearl: Central cord syndrome (hyperextension / syrinx): Upper extremity weakness > Lower extremity weakness (cervical fibers lie medially in corticospinal tract) + cape-like pain/temp loss.

source: Content Q13: Subacute Combined Degeneration (Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
question: A 58-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis and autoimmune gastritis presents with progressive numbness and tingling in both feet, unsteady gait, and leg stiffness over 6 months. Physical exam reveals: absent vibration sense up to the iliac crests, impaired joint position sense, a positive Romberg sign (sways and falls when eyes are closed), 4+ hyperactive knee jerks, bilateral ankle clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign). Laboratory evaluation demonstrates macrocytic anemia and elevated serum methylmalonic acid. Which tracts in the spinal cord are demyelinated in Subacute Combined Degeneration?

options.text: Dorsal columns (sensory ataxia) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic paraparesis)
Anterior white commissure and anterior corticospinal tracts exclusively
Spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn motor neurons exclusively
Rubrospinal tracts and tectospinal tracts in the brainstem tegmentum
Spinocerebellar tracts and sympathetic intermediolateral cell columns exclusively

explanation: Subacute Combined Degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord is caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (often secondary to pernicious anemia / autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells producing intrinsic factor). Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; its deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid, leading to defective myelin synthesis and vacuolar degeneration. The classic histological pattern is bilateral demyelination of: 1) Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) $\rightarrow$ loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign. 2) Lateral corticospinal tracts $\rightarrow$ spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs. Associated peripheral neuropathy produces 'glove-and-stocking' paresthesias.
high_yield_pearl: Subacute Combined Degeneration (B12 deficiency): Demyelination of Dorsal Columns (proprioception/vibration loss, +Romberg) + Lateral Corticospinal Tracts (spastic weakness, +Babinski).

source: Content Q13: Poliomyelitis (Anterior Horn Cell LMN Disease)
question: A 4-year-old unimmunized child from an endemic region presents with fever, headache, stiff neck, and vomiting. Three days later, the child develops acute flaccid paralysis of the right leg. Examination shows marked hypotonia and complete absence of the right patellar and Achilles reflexes, with normal sensation to pinprick and light touch across the entire body. Lumbar puncture demonstrates a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which cellular structure is selectively destroyed by this enteroviral infection?

options.text: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons within the paravertebral chain
Alpha motor neurons in the anterior (ventral) horns of the spinal cord
Pseudounipolar sensory neurons in the lumbar dorsal root ganglia
Oligodendrocytes within the lateral funiculus of the thoracic spinal cord
Astrocytic foot processes forming the blood-brain barrier interface

explanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by the poliovirus (a single-stranded positive-sense RNA enterovirus of the Picornaviridae family). The virus spreads hematogenously to the central nervous system, where it exhibits selective tropism for lower motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord (and motor cranial nerve nuclei in bulbar polio). Destruction of anterior horn cells produces pure Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) deficits: asymmetric flaccid paralysis, severe muscle weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, and subsequent muscle atrophy. Sensation is completely spared because dorsal root ganglia and sensory tracts are untouched.
high_yield_pearl: Poliomyelitis: Enterovirus destroys anterior horn cells $\rightarrow$ asymmetric pure LMN flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and atrophy with PRESERVED sensation.

source: Content Q13: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA)
question: A 3-month-old infant boy is evaluated for severe generalized hypotonia and muscle weakness ('floppy baby'). His mother reports that he has a weak cry, breathes with paradoxical bell-shaped abdominal movements, and has difficulty breastfeeding. On examination, the infant cannot lift his head, has absent deep tendon reflexes, and demonstrates fine, continuous fasciculations of the tongue. Molecular genetic testing confirms a homozygous deletion of the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5q. What is the pathological mechanism of this disorder?

options.text: Failure of lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity leading to histiocytic lipid storage
Accumulation of phytanic acid within peripheral nerve myelin sheaths
Autoimmune antibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic muscle acetylcholine receptors
Defective dystrophin cytoskeletal anchoring leading to progressive sarcolemmal tearing
Degeneration and loss of anterior horn lower motor neurons due to survival motor neuron protein deficiency

explanation: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA, Werdnig-Hoffmann disease / Type 1 SMA) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by homozygous mutations or deletions in the SMN1 (survival motor neuron 1) gene on chromosome 5q13. SMN protein is critical for snRNP assembly in the spliceosome; its deficiency leads to selective apoptosis and progressive loss of anterior horn lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. Infants present within the first 6 months of life with severe progressive hypotonia ('floppy infant'), symmetric proximal flaccid weakness, areflexia, bell-shaped chest due to intercostal weakness with diaphragmatic breathing, and pathognomonic tongue fasciculations.
high_yield_pearl: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA, SMN1 mutation on 5q): Degeneration of anterior horn cells $\rightarrow$ 'floppy baby' with hypotonia, areflexia, and tongue fasciculations.

source: Content Q13: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
question: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and muscle stiffness that began in his right hand and has now spread to his left arm and both legs over the past 9 months. Neurological examination reveals: severe atrophy and visible fasciculations in the intrinsic hand muscles and tongue (LMN signs), combined with bilateral hyperactive 4+ patellar reflexes, sustained ankle clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses (UMN signs). Sensation, eye movements, and bowel/bladder control are completely normal. What is the diagnosis, and which neuroprotective medication prolongs survival by inhibiting glutamate release?

options.text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS); treated with riluzole, which reduces excitotoxic glutamate neurotransmission
Myasthenia gravis; treated with pyridostigmine, which inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the motor endplate
Parkinson disease; treated with carbidopa-levodopa to replace striatal dopamine deficiency
Guillain-Barré syndrome; treated with intravenous immunoglobulin to neutralize anti-ganglioside antibodies
Multiple sclerosis; treated with natalizumab, which blocks alpha-4 integrin leukocyte extravasation

explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig's disease) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by combined Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) and Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) degeneration: 1) LMN signs: muscle wasting/atrophy, weakness, fasciculations, and fibrillations. 2) UMN signs: spasticity, hyperactive reflexes, clonus, and positive Babinski signs. Pathognomonic clinical hallmark: co-existence of UMN and LMN signs in the same limb or myotome (e.g., hyperactive reflexes in a wasted, fasciculating limb). Sensation, bowel/bladder sphincters, and extraocular muscles (CN III, IV, VI) are characteristically spared. First-line therapy is riluzole (a glutamate antagonist that decreases glutamate release and excitotoxicity, extending survival by several months) and edaravone (a free radical scavenger).
high_yield_pearl: ALS: Combined UMN (spasticity, +Babinski, hyperreflexia) + LMN (atrophy, fasciculations) signs with normal sensation. Treat: Riluzole (decreases glutamate excitotoxicity).

source: Content Q13: Tabes Dorsalis (Neurosyphilis)
question: A 63-year-old man presents with severe, shooting, 'lightning-like' pains in his lower limbs, difficulty walking in the dark, and progressive urinary incontinence. Physical exam reveals a wide-based, stomping 'steppage' gait and a positive Romberg sign. Bilateral patellar and Achilles reflexes are completely absent. Testing reveals total loss of vibration and joint position sense in both lower extremities, with intact pinprick sensation. Both pupils are small and constrict briskly to accommodation but do not react to direct light (Argyll Robertson pupils). Which spinal cord structure is destroyed in this patient's tabes dorsalis?

options.text: Ventral white commissure and spinothalamic tracts due to central cavitary syringomyelia
Pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla due to atherothrombotic basilar artery disease
Dorsal roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) due to tertiary Treponema pallidum infection
Anterior horn motor neurons and lateral corticospinal tracts due to enteroviral neurotropism
Lateral spinothalamic tracts and descending autonomic sympathetic fibers in the brainstem

explanation: Tabes dorsalis is a late manifestation of tertiary neurosyphilis caused by Treponema pallidum spirochetal infection. It involves chronic progressive inflammatory degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia and demyelination of the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) in the spinal cord. Clinical hallmarks: 1) Loss of proprioception and vibration sense $\rightarrow$ sensory ataxia, wide-based stomping gait, and a positive Romberg sign (swaying/falling with eyes closed). 2) Severe, paroxysmal, lancinating ('lightning') pains in legs and abdomen. 3) Areflexia (loss of sensory limb of stretch reflex). 4) Neurotrophic joint destruction (Charcot joints). 5) Bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils ('prostitute's pupils': Accommodate but do Not React to light).
high_yield_pearl: Tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis): Demyelination of dorsal roots & dorsal columns $\rightarrow$ sensory ataxia, +Romberg, loss of proprioception/reflexes + Argyll Robertson pupils.

source: Content Q13: Cauda Equina vs. Conus Medullaris Syndrome
question: A 45-year-old construction worker with a massive acute central disc herniation at the L4-L5 level presents with severe lower back pain radiating down both legs. Examination reveals asymmetric flaccid weakness of foot dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally, patchy 'saddle anesthesia' over the perineum and buttocks, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. How does this Cauda Equina Syndrome fundamentally differ from Conus Medullaris Syndrome?

options.text: Cauda equina syndrome involves LMN compression of lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus (L2), producing asymmetric flaccid deficits
Cauda equina syndrome causes isolated loss of upper extremity reflexes while sparing the lower extremities entirely
Cauda equina syndrome is characterized by early, prominent symmetric perianal sensory loss and early bowel incontinence
Cauda equina syndrome is an emergency caused by thrombosis of the superior sagittal venous sinus
Cauda equina syndrome involves pure UMN compression of the terminal spinal cord at T10, producing hyperreflexia

explanation: The spinal cord terminates as the conus medullaris at the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults; below L2, the lumbar cistern contains the lumbosacral nerve roots (the cauda equina). Cauda Equina Syndrome results from compression of these nerve roots (L3-S5) below the conus (commonly massive central disc herniation at L4-L5 or L5-S1). Because nerve roots are peripheral nerves, it is a Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) disorder: asymmetric, patchy flaccid leg weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia, asymmetric saddle anesthesia, severe radicular pain, and later-onset bowel/bladder dysfunction. In contrast, Conus Medullaris Syndrome (lesion at L1-L2 vertebra) damages the terminal spinal cord directly: it presents with symmetric perineal numbness, early and prominent urinary/fecal incontinence, symmetric mild leg weakness, and mixed UMN/LMN signs.
high_yield_pearl: Cauda equina syndrome: LMN lesion below L2 (nerve roots) $\rightarrow$ ASYMMETRIC flaccid weakness, areflexia, saddle anesthesia, severe pain, late incontinence. Emergency decompression.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 9, 31 & Content Q1: Muscle Spindles vs. Golgi Tendon Organs
question: During clinical reflex testing, two specialized sensory receptors monitor muscle mechanics: muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs). Which statement accurately compares their anatomical arrangement, primary mechanical stimulus, and functional reflex role?

options.text: Muscle spindles detect changes in chemical ATP concentration; Golgi tendon organs detect extracellular potassium ion accumulation
Muscle spindles inhibit alpha motor neurons during maximal load; Golgi tendon organs stimulate gamma motor neurons during rapid stretch
Muscle spindles are arranged in parallel with muscle fibers to detect stretch; Golgi tendon organs are arranged in series to detect tension
Muscle spindles are in series within the tendon to detect contraction force; Golgi tendon organs are in parallel within the belly to detect length
Muscle spindles are innervated by group Ib afferents; Golgi tendon organs are innervated exclusively by group Ia afferents

explanation: Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) serve complementary proprioceptive functions: 1) Muscle spindles are located within the fleshy belly of skeletal muscle and are arranged IN PARALLEL with extrafusal muscle fibers. They are innervated by group Ia and II afferent fibers (and gamma motor efferents). They detect changes in muscle LENGTH and rate of change of length (stretch). Stretching the muscle activates spindles, triggering the monosynaptic myotatic stretch reflex (alpha motor neuron activation $\rightarrow$ muscle contraction). 2) Golgi tendon organs are encapsulated sensory receptors located at the musculotendinous junction, arranged IN SERIES with muscle fibers. They are innervated by group Ib sensory afferents and detect muscle TENSION (contractile force). Excessive tension stimulates GTOs, activating inhibitory spinal interneurons that relax the contracting muscle (inverse myotatic reflex / autogenic inhibition, protecting the tendon from tearing).
high_yield_pearl: Muscle spindles = in PARALLEL, detect length/stretch (Ia afferents $\rightarrow$ stretch reflex). Golgi tendon organs = in SERIES, detect tension/force (Ib afferents $\rightarrow$ autogenic inhibition).

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 30-31 & Content Q2: Clonus Neurophysiology
question: During a physical examination of a stroke patient with spastic hemiparesis, the neurologist rapidly dorsiflexes the patient's foot at the ankle and holds it under gentle sustained pressure. The foot responds with rhythmic, alternating, involuntary contractions at a frequency of 5 to 7 Hz that persist as long as the foot is held dorsiflexed (sustained ankle clonus). What is the neurophysiological origin of this clinical sign?

options.text: Spontaneous activation of the Golgi tendon organ Ib afferent fibers within the Achilles tendon
Periodic obstruction of venous blood flow through the deep calf veins causing muscle ischemia
Rhythmic pacemaking activity originating in the ischemic cerebellar dentate nucleus
Continuous electrical discharge from denervated muscle fibers due to acetylcholine supersensitivity
A self-perpetuating, disinhibited stretch reflex cycle driven by uninhibited spinal hyperreflexia

explanation: Clonus is a series of involuntary, rhythmic, oscillatory muscle contractions and relaxations (typically 5 to 7 Hz) elicited by sudden, sustained passive stretching of a muscle-tendon unit (most readily elicited at the ankle by rapid dorsiflexion, or at the patella). In a healthy individual, descending supraspinal tracts inhibit reflex oscillations after 1 or 2 beats. In a patient with an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion, loss of descending cortical and reticulospinal inhibition causes profound spinal hyperreflexia: the initial stretch elicits a reflex contraction, which relaxes and immediately restretches the spindle, triggering an autonomous, self-re-exciting loop of rhythmic contractions that continues as long as the stretch is maintained. Sustained clonus ($\ge$5 beats) is always pathological.
high_yield_pearl: Clonus: Sustained rhythmic oscillatory contractions elicited by sudden passive stretch $\rightarrow$ pathognomonic UMN sign caused by disinhibited self-perpetuating stretch reflex arcs.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 16-18 & Content Q8: Premotor Cortex vs. Supplementary Motor Area
question: The motor planning areas in the frontal lobe (Brodmann area 6) are divided into the lateral premotor cortex and the medial supplementary motor area (SMA). A neuroscientist records single-unit activity in a non-human primate executing different motor paradigms. Which functional distinction differentiates the roles of the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area?

options.text: Premotor cortex innervates cranial nerve motor nuclei; the supplementary motor area innervates only the sacral parasympathetic nucleus
Premotor cortex coordinates motor acts guided by external sensory cues; the supplementary motor area plans internally generated complex sequences
Premotor cortex is active only during sleep; the supplementary motor area is active only during intense awake concentration
Premotor cortex generates the cardiac rhythm; the supplementary motor area controls involuntary smooth muscle peristalsis
Premotor cortex is dedicated exclusively to sensory perception; the supplementary motor area executes all involuntary vegetative reflexes

explanation: Both the lateral premotor cortex (PMA) and the medial supplementary motor area (SMA) occupy Brodmann area 6 anterior to the primary motor cortex (area 4) and project to area 4 and the corticospinal tract. 1) Premotor cortex (lateral area 6): Specialized for planning, preparing, and guiding movements that are triggered or guided by EXTERNAL sensory cues (e.g., reaching for a visually presented red cup, or stopping a car in response to a red traffic light). 2) Supplementary motor area (medial area 6): Specialized for planning and initiating INTERNALLY generated movements, memorized motor routines, and complex bimanual coordination (e.g., mentally rehearsing or executing a memorized piano sequence without external cues).
high_yield_pearl: Premotor cortex (lateral area 6) = movements guided by EXTERNAL sensory cues. Supplementary motor area (medial area 6) = INTERNALLY generated complex sequences.

source: Lecture File 14 Slide 13-14 & Content Q8: Motor Cortex Vascular Supply & Homunculus
question: A 74-year-old man with carotid artery stenosis suffers an acute ischemic stroke. Examination reveals severe spastic hemiparesis affecting his right face, tongue, and right arm, whereas motor strength in his right leg and foot is completely preserved (5/5). He also exhibits expressive Broca's aphasia. Which cerebral artery was occluded, and which specific territory of the primary motor cortex homunculus did it perfuse?

options.text: Left anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which perfuses the medial surface of the precentral gyrus representing the leg and foot
Basilar artery trunk, which perfuses the paramedian tegmentum of the rostral pons and midbrain
Left posterior cerebral artery (PCA), which perfuses the occipital pole and ventral parahippocampal gyrus
Left anterior choroidal artery, which perfuses the entire hippocampus and lateral geniculate nucleus
Left middle cerebral artery (MCA), which perfuses the lateral convexity of the precentral gyrus representing the face and arm

explanation: The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4) has an inverted somatotopic 'motor homunculus' that is divided into two distinct arterial vascular territories: 1) The lateral convexity of the precentral gyrus represents the face, tongue, larynx, hand, arm, and trunk; it is supplied by the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). Occlusion of the superior division of the left MCA produces contralateral weakness of the face and arm with sparing of the leg, along with Broca's expressive aphasia. 2) The medial surface of the hemisphere (within the longitudinal fissure) and the paracentral lobule represent the lower extremity (hip, leg, foot, and perineum); it is supplied by the Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA). Occlusion of the ACA produces contralateral motor and sensory loss confined to the leg and foot, with sparing of the face and arm.
high_yield_pearl: Motor homunculus vascular territories: MCA supplies lateral convexity (Face & Arm). ACA supplies medial cortex / paracentral lobule (Leg & Foot).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: Wakefulness EEG
question: A healthy 25-year-old medical student participates in an electroencephalography (EEG) laboratory exercise. When she sits alert and attentive with her eyes open reading a textbook, the EEG demonstrates high-frequency, low-amplitude desynchronized beta waves. When she is instructed to close her eyes, relax, and remain awake, a distinct synchronous rhythm appears over the posterior occipital scalp. Which waveform characterizes this relaxed, eyes-closed wakeful state?

options.text: Delta waves with a frequency of less than 4 Hz and high amplitude voltage
Sawtooth waves with a frequency of 2 to 6 Hz synchronized with conjugate eye bursts
Sleep spindles with a frequency of 12 to 14 Hz bursting every few seconds
Alpha waves with a frequency of 8 to 13 Hz, predominantly localized to the occipital leads
Theta waves with a frequency of 4 to 7 Hz accompanied by vertex sharp waves

explanation: Electroencephalography of wakefulness demonstrates two distinct physiologic states: 1) Active, alert wakefulness with eyes open: characterized by Beta waves (high frequency >13 Hz [typically 13-30 Hz], low voltage, desynchronized rhythm), reflecting active cortical processing. 2) Relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed: characterized by Alpha waves (frequency of 8 to 13 Hz, synchronous, moderate amplitude), which are most prominent over the posterior occipital and parietal regions (the posterior dominant rhythm). Opening the eyes produces immediate alpha block (attenuation of alpha waves replaced by beta waves).
high_yield_pearl: Wakefulness EEG: Eyes open/alert = Beta waves (>13 Hz, desynchronized). Eyes closed/relaxed = Alpha waves (8-13 Hz, occipital dominant).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: Stage N1 Sleep
question: During an overnight polysomnogram, a patient begins to drift from wakefulness into the lightest stage of Non-REM sleep (Stage N1). The alpha rhythm disappears from the occipital leads. What replaces the alpha rhythm on the EEG, and which characteristic eye movements and somatic phenomena are typically observed during Stage N1 sleep?

options.text: Sleep spindles (12 to 14 Hz), absence of eye movements, and sustained alveolar hyperventilation
Sawtooth waves, complete pupillary dilation, and continuous rhythmic teeth grinding
High-voltage spikes, sustained ankle clonus, and paroxysmal nocturnal vocalizations
Theta waves (4 to 7 Hz), slow rolling conjugate eye movements, and occasional hypnic jerks
Delta waves (< 4 Hz), rapid saccadic eye movements, and generalized skeletal muscle atonia

explanation: Stage N1 (light transition sleep) accounts for approximately 4% to 5% of total sleep time. As the patient transitions from wakefulness into N1 sleep, the background alpha rhythm attenuates and is replaced by low-amplitude, mixed-frequency Theta waves (4 to 7 Hz). Polysomnography demonstrates slow, rolling conjugate eye movements on electrooculography (EOG) and mild reduction in submental muscle tone. Individuals frequently experience hypnic jerks (sleep starts, sudden involuntary myoclonic twitches of the limbs or body often accompanied by a sensation of falling) and vertex sharp waves near the end of N1.
high_yield_pearl: Stage N1 Sleep: Lightest sleep (~5%). EEG = Theta waves (4-7 Hz). Features: Slow rolling eye movements & hypnic jerks.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: Stage N2 Sleep
question: A 40-year-old man undergoes overnight diagnostic polysomnography. The sleep technician observes that the patient spends the largest proportion of the night in a specific Non-REM sleep stage characterized on the EEG by intermittent bursts of 12 to 14 Hz sinusoidal waves and high-voltage, biphasic sharp waves. Which stage of sleep is this, which EEG features define it, and what thalamic structure generates these bursts?

options.text: Stage REM sleep, defined by ponto-geniculo-occipital spikes generated by the dorsal raphe nucleus
Stage N3 sleep, defined by synchronized delta waves generated by the anterior hypothalamus
Stage N2 sleep, defined by sleep spindles generated by the reticular thalamic nucleus and K-complexes
Stage N1 sleep, defined by vertex sharp transients generated by the cerebellar dentate nucleus
Awake state, defined by mu rhythms generated by the primary motor cortex hand representation

explanation: Stage N2 sleep comprises the largest proportion of normal adult sleep (approximately 45% to 55% of total sleep time). It is electrophysiologically defined by two signature waveforms: 1) Sleep spindles: brief, 0.5- to 1.5-second bursts of 12 to 14 Hz sinusoidal activity generated by rhythmic burst-firing of GABAergic neurons in the reticular nucleus of the thalamus, which functionally disconnects the cerebral cortex from sensory inputs. 2) K-complexes: isolated, high-voltage biphasic waves ($\ge$0.5 seconds duration) with an initial negative sharp deflection followed by a positive component. Bruxism (teeth grinding) typically occurs in Stage N2.
high_yield_pearl: Stage N2 Sleep: Largest percentage of sleep (~50%). Hallmarks: Sleep spindles (12-14 Hz, thalamic reticular nucleus) & K-complexes. Bruxism occurs here.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: Stage N3 Sleep (Slow-Wave Sleep)
question: During the first third of the night, a healthy 18-year-old athlete enters deep, slow-wave sleep (Stage N3). A hypnogram illustrates this stage with high-amplitude, low-frequency waveforms. Which physiological endocrine and neurological characteristics define Stage N3 sleep?

options.text: Desynchronized EEG, continuous penile tumescence, and rapid saccadic eye movements
Delta waves (< 4 Hz), peak secretion of growth hormone and prolactin, and the occurrence of sleep terrors and sleepwalking
Beta waves (> 13 Hz), maximal cerebral oxygen consumption, and voluntary limb locomotion
Theta waves (4 to 7 Hz), selective release of cortisol and glucagon, and dream mentation with muscle atonia
Sleep spindles, suppression of all pituitary hormones, and episodic Cheyne-Stokes breathing

explanation: Stage N3 (Slow-Wave Sleep / Deep Sleep) comprises approximately 15% to 20% of total sleep time and occurs predominantly during the first third of the night. On EEG, it is defined by synchronized Delta waves (frequency <4 Hz, high voltage >75 $\mu$V) occupying $\ge$20% of the epoch. Physiological hallmarks: peak pulsatile secretion of growth hormone (GH) and prolactin, lowest cerebral metabolic rate, lowest blood pressure, and lowest heart rate. Awakening from N3 causes severe grogginess ('sleep inertia'). Crucially, N3 is the stage where Non-REM parasomnias occur: sleepwalking (somnambulism), sleep terrors (night terrors), and nocturnal enuresis.
high_yield_pearl: Stage N3 (Slow-Wave Sleep): Delta waves (<4 Hz). First 1/3 of night. Peak Growth Hormone & Prolactin release. Site of sleepwalking & night terrors.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: REM Sleep Physiology
question: During Stage REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, the brain exhibits a paradoxically active metabolic and electrical profile despite the individual being in a state of profound behavioral sleep. Which constellation of neurophysiological features defines normal REM sleep?

options.text: Prominent alpha rhythm, slow rolling eye movements, shivering thermogenesis, and sleep terrors
Continuous sleep spindles, unilateral pupillary dilation, active leg locomotion, and growth hormone secretion
Isoelectric flatline EEG, fixed non-reactive pupils, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, and bruxism
High-voltage synchronized delta waves, absent eye movements, skeletal muscle hypertonia, and no dreams
Desynchronized mixed-frequency EEG with sawtooth waves, conjugate rapid eye movements, generalized muscle atonia, and dreaming

explanation: Stage REM (Rapid Eye Movement sleep, or 'paradoxical sleep') constitutes approximately 20% to 25% of total sleep time, recurring in 90- to 120-minute cycles that become progressively longer toward morning. Characteristics: 1) EEG: desynchronized, low-voltage, mixed-frequency background with characteristic triangular 'sawtooth waves' (2 to 6 Hz). 2) EOG: rapid, irregular, conjugate eye movements (driven by PPRF and superior colliculus). 3) EMG: profound generalized skeletal muscle atonia (paralysis), which prevents acting out dreams. 4) Mentation: vivid, narrative, emotional dreaming. 5) Autonomic instability: fluctuating heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate; penile or clitoral tumescence; elevated brain oxygen consumption and cerebral blood flow.
high_yield_pearl: Stage REM Sleep: 'Paradoxical sleep' (~25%). Desynchronized EEG + sawtooth waves, rapid eye movements, muscle ATONIA, vivid dreams, penile tumescence.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: REM Sleep Atonia Circuitry
question: During normal REM sleep, skeletal muscles throughout the body are completely paralyzed (atonia), with two crucial exceptions: the extraocular muscles and the diaphragm. Which brainstem nucleus and neurotransmitters are responsible for generating this motor atonia during REM sleep?

options.text: Edinger-Westphal nucleus releasing acetylcholine to contract the ciliary muscle continuously
Sublaterodorsal nucleus in the pons activating glycinergic and GABAergic premotor neurons that inhibit spinal alpha motor neurons
Locus coeruleus releasing norepinephrine to hyperpolarize primary muscle spindle afferents
Substantia nigra pars reticulata releasing dopamine directly onto neuromuscular junction nicotinic receptors
Dorsal raphe nucleus releasing serotonin to block voltage-gated sodium channels in the corticospinal tract

explanation: Skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep is mediated by an active brainstem inhibitory circuit: Cholinergic/glutamatergic neurons in the pontine tegmentum (specifically the sublaterodorsal nucleus, SLD, or nucleus pontis oralis) project to premotor inhibitory neurons in the ventromedial medulla and spinal cord. These inhibitory interneurons release the neurotransmitters glycine and GABA onto somatic alpha motor neurons, profoundly hyperpolarizing their membranes and producing postsynaptic flaccid atonia. This prevents motor execution of dream mentation. Sparing of somatic motor neurons to the diaphragm (phrenic C3-C5) and extraocular muscles (CN III, IV, VI) permits continuous breathing and rapid eye movements.
high_yield_pearl: REM atonia circuit: Pontine sublaterodorsal nucleus $\rightarrow$ ventromedial medulla $\rightarrow$ Glycine and GABA release inhibits spinal alpha motor neurons (spares diaphragm & EOM).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2 & Content Q1: Sleep Changes with Aging
question: An 80-year-old woman reports that she wakes up frequently during the night, feels sleepy earlier in the evening, and wakes up wide awake at 4:30 AM every morning. Polysomnography confirms age-related changes in her sleep architecture. Which alterations in sleep stages characteristically occur as a normal consequence of healthy aging?

options.text: Marked decrease or near-absence of Stage N3 slow-wave sleep, decreased REM sleep, and increased sleep fragmentation
Development of continuous generalized muscle atonia throughout all Non-REM sleep cycles
Selective abolition of Stage N1 sleep with normal duration of all other Non-REM sleep stages
Dramatic increase in Stage N3 slow-wave sleep, complete absence of Stage N2 sleep, and total sleep time of 12 hours
Prolongation of the initial REM period to three hours with total suppression of sleep spindles

explanation: Normal aging is accompanied by substantial, predictable changes in sleep architecture: 1) Marked reduction in deep, slow-wave sleep: Stage N3 sleep declines significantly and may be completely absent in elderly adults. 2) Mild decrease in total REM sleep percentage. 3) Increase in light sleep: Stages N1 and N2 increase proportionally. 4) Increased sleep fragmentation: frequent nighttime awakenings (wake after sleep onset / WASO) due to nocturia, pain, or decreased sleep efficiency. 5) Advanced sleep phase: shift toward earlier sleep-onset times (falling asleep by 7-9 PM) and early morning awakenings (waking at 3-5 AM). 6) Decreased total nocturnal sleep duration with compensatory daytime napping.
high_yield_pearl: Sleep in elderly: Marked decrease in Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep), decreased REM sleep, increased wakefulness/fragmentation, earlier sleep phase.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 3 & Content Q2: Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)
question: The 24-hour circadian rhythm of the human sleep-wake cycle is coordinated by a master pacemaker in the brain that synchronizes internal physiology with external environmental light-dark cycles. Which hypothalamic nucleus serves as this master circadian clock, and via which dedicated pathway does it receive photic entrainment?

options.text: Suprachiasmatic nucleus in the anterior hypothalamus, receiving input from melanopsin retinal ganglion cells via the retinohypothalamic tract
Lateral hypothalamic area in the posterior zone, receiving gustatory sensory input from solitary tract nuclei to drive appetite stimulation
Ventromedial nucleus in the middle hypothalamus, receiving auditory signals from cochlear pathways to regulate satiety and food intake
Mammillary body in the posterior hypothalamus, receiving limbic memory projections through the fornix to consolidate episodic recollections
Arcuate nucleus in the tuberal hypothalamus, receiving visceral spinothalamic sensations to regulate neuroendocrine pituitary secretions

explanation: The Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN), located in the anterior hypothalamus immediately superior to the optic chiasm, is the master circadian pacemaker in mammals. It contains an intrinsic autonomous molecular clock driven by autoregulatory transcriptional feedback loops (CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY genes). To entrain this ~24.2-hour endogenous rhythm to the solar 24-hour day, the SCN receives direct photic input via the retinohypothalamic tract from intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) that contain the photopigment melanopsin, independent of rod and cone conscious vision.
high_yield_pearl: Master circadian pacemaker = Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN) of anterior hypothalamus. Entrained by light via retinohypothalamic tract (melanopsin ipRGCs).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 3 & Content Q2: Pineal Gland & Melatonin Circuit
question: Melatonin is a hormone synthesized by the pineal gland that promotes sleepiness and circadian phase shifts. During daylight, light reaching the retina suppresses melatonin production; in darkness, melatonin synthesis surges. Which multi-synaptic sympathetic pathway connects the master circadian clock to the pineal gland to control melatonin secretion?

options.text: SCN -> Optic tract -> Edinger-Westphal nucleus -> Ciliary ganglion -> Pineal gland
SCN -> Stria terminalis -> Medial amygdala -> Submandibular ganglion -> Pineal gland
SCN -> Medial forebrain bundle -> Ventral tegmental area -> Otic ganglion -> Pineal gland
SCN -> Dorsal longitudinal fasciculus -> Dorsal vagal motor nucleus -> Celiac ganglion -> Pineal gland
SCN -> Paraventricular nucleus -> Intermediolateral cell column (C8-T2) -> Superior cervical ganglion -> Pineal gland

explanation: The neural pathway regulating melatonin synthesis is multi-synaptic: 1) Light activates ipRGCs in the retina $\rightarrow$ retinohypothalamic tract $\rightarrow$ Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN). 2) SCN GABAergic neurons project to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus, inhibiting its output during daylight. 3) In darkness, SCN inhibition ceases, allowing the PVN to stimulate preganglionic sympathetic neurons in the intermediolateral cell column (IML) of the upper thoracic spinal cord (C8-T2). 4) Sympathetic preganglionics project to the Superior Cervical Ganglion (SCG). 5) Postganglionic noradrenergic sympathetic fibers ascend along blood vessels to innervate pinealocytes in the pineal gland. Norepinephrine acts on beta-1 adrenergic receptors to activate arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT), converting serotonin to melatonin.
high_yield_pearl: Melatonin pathway: Light inhibits SCN $\rightarrow$ darkness disinhibits PVN $\rightarrow$ IML (C8-T2) $\rightarrow$ Superior Cervical Ganglion $\rightarrow$ Pineal gland releases melatonin.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 3 & Content Q2: Ventrolateral Preoptic Nucleus (VLPO)
question: A 52-year-old man sustains an ischemic stroke affecting the anterior hypothalamus. Following the stroke, he develops profound, severe insomnia, sleeping less than two hours per 24-hour period. Destruction of which specific hypothalamic 'sleep switch' center explains his inability to initiate and maintain sleep?

options.text: Lateral hypothalamic area, which uses orexin to stimulate the locus coeruleus and raphe
Posterior hypothalamic nucleus, which uses dopamine to maintain conscious wakefulness
Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO), which uses GABA and galanin to inhibit wake-promoting arousal centers
Supraoptic nucleus, which secretes oxytocin and vasopressin into the systemic circulation
Tuberomammillary nucleus, which uses histamine to excite the thalamic reticular nucleus

explanation: The Ventrolateral Preoptic Nucleus (VLPO), located in the anterior hypothalamus, is the primary sleep-promoting center ('sleep switch') in the brain. VLPO neurons are 'sleep-active': they increase their firing rate during Non-REM and REM sleep. They send inhibitory projections containing the neurotransmitters GABA and galanin to all major components of the Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) wake-promoting centers (including the locus coeruleus [NE], dorsal raphe [5-HT], tuberomammillary nucleus [histamine], and PPT/LDT [ACh]). Destruction of the VLPO abolishes this physiological sleep drive, resulting in profound, intractable insomnia.
high_yield_pearl: VLPO (anterior hypothalamus) = Main sleep-promoting center ('sleep switch'). Releases GABA & galanin to inhibit ARAS wake centers.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 3 & Content Q2: ARAS & Antihistamine Sedation
question: A 28-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine (an over-the-counter first-generation H1 receptor antihistamine) for seasonal allergic rhinitis. Within 45 minutes, she experiences intense, overwhelming drowsiness and falls asleep on the couch. Which component of the Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) is inhibited by this medication to cause sedation?

options.text: Pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus, which provides wake-promoting cholinergic projections
Substantia nigra pars compacta, which provides wake-promoting dopaminergic projections
Tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus, which provides wake-promoting histaminergic projections
Dorsal raphe nucleus in the rostral midbrain, which provides wake-promoting serotonergic projections
Locus coeruleus in the dorsal pons, which provides wake-promoting noradrenergic projections

explanation: The Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) maintains conscious cortical arousal via several distinct monoaminergic and cholinergic projections: 1) Locus coeruleus: Norepinephrine (NE). 2) Dorsal raphe nuclei: Serotonin (5-HT). 3) Tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) of the posterior hypothalamus: Histamine. 4) Pedunculopontine (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) nuclei & basal forebrain: Acetylcholine (ACh). First-generation H1 antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine) are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier to competitively block central H1 receptors in the cortex and thalamus, suppressing TMN histaminergic arousal and causing marked sedation. Second-generation antihistamines (e.g., loratadine, cetirizine) do not cross the blood-brain barrier and are non-sedating.
high_yield_pearl: ARAS histaminergic center = Tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) of posterior hypothalamus. 1st-gen antihistamines cross BBB $\rightarrow$ block H1 $\rightarrow$ sedation.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 3 & Content Q2: Orexin (Hypocretin) Neurobiology
question: Orexin-A and orexin-B (also known as hypocretin-1 and hypocretin-2) are excitatory neuropeptides synthesized exclusively by a discrete cluster of neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area. What is the fundamental neurobiological role of the orexin system in the control of sleep and wakefulness?

options.text: Inducing skeletal muscle atonia during Stage N2 sleep by releasing glycine onto motor neurons
Stabilizing the sleep-wake flip-flop switch by exciting monoaminergic arousal centers to maintain sustained wakefulness
Stimulating pinealocytes to synthesize melatonin during daytime exposure to solar ultraviolet light
Clearing toxic amyloid-beta oligomers from the cerebral interstitial space during deep sleep
Directly inhibiting the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus to initiate deep Stage N3 slow-wave sleep

explanation: The orexin (hypocretin) system is essential for maintaining sustained, consolidated wakefulness and stabilizing the 'flip-flop switch' between wakefulness and sleep. Orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area project broadly to and powerfully excite all components of the ARAS (locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe, tuberomammillary nucleus, and cholinergic basal forebrain). By keeping these wake-promoting nuclei tonically active during the day, orexin prevents inappropriate, sudden transitions into Non-REM or REM sleep. Loss of orexin leads to behavioral state instability (narcolepsy).
high_yield_pearl: Orexin / Hypocretin (lateral hypothalamus): Excites monoaminergic ARAS centers to stabilize the sleep-wake switch $\rightarrow$ maintains consolidated wakefulness.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 1: Narcolepsy Type 1 Pathophysiology
question: An 18-year-old female presents with severe, unyielding daytime sleepiness, falling asleep in the middle of conversations and during examinations. She undergoes genetic testing and diagnostic lumbar puncture. Testing reveals the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele and a cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) concentration of less than 40 pg/mL (normal: >200 pg/mL). What is the underlying neuropathological mechanism of Narcolepsy Type 1?

options.text: Diffuse demyelinating plaques centered on the bilateral internal capsules
Selective autoimmune destruction of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area
Bilateral ischemic infarction of the ventral anterior thalamic relay nuclei
Chronic enteroviral infection of cholinergic motor neurons in the spinal cord
Prion-mediated vacuolar degeneration of the suprachiasmatic nucleus

explanation: Narcolepsy Type 1 (narcolepsy with cataplexy) is an autoimmune neurodegenerative disorder. In genetically predisposed individuals (strongly associated with the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele, present in >98% of patients, and often triggered by seasonal influenza or Streptococcus pyogenes infection), autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes selectively destroy the ~70,000 orexin/hypocretin-synthesizing neurons located in the lateral hypothalamic area. Loss of orexinergic stabilization produces hallmark CSF hypocretin-1 levels <110 pg/mL (or <1/3 normal mean) and destabilizes the sleep-wake switch.
high_yield_pearl: Narcolepsy Type 1: Autoimmune destruction of orexin/hypocretin neurons in lateral hypothalamus (HLA-DQB1*06:02). CSF hypocretin-1 < 110 pg/mL.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 1: Narcolepsy Clinical Tetrad
question: A 20-year-old college student presents with excessive daytime sleepiness despite sleeping 8 hours every night. While telling a humorous joke to friends, his knees suddenly buckle, his head drops forward, and he collapses to the floor for 30 seconds; throughout this episode, he remains fully conscious and aware of his surroundings. He also reports terrifying episodes where he sees shadowy intruders at the foot of his bed just as he falls asleep, accompanied by an inability to move any of his limbs for 1 to 2 minutes upon waking. What clinical tetrad defines this disorder?

options.text: Violent acting out of dreams, visual hallucinations, parkinsonian resting tremor, and dementia
Bilateral aching leg dysesthesias, nocturnal teeth grinding, sleep enuresis, and weight loss
Loud snoring, daytime hypercapnia, secondary erythrocytosis, and morning headaches
Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis
Insomnia, night terrors, sleepwalking, and morning confusional arousals

explanation: The classic clinical tetrad of Narcolepsy consists of: 1) Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS): unavoidable 'sleep attacks' that occur during sedentary or active situations (mandatory feature). 2) Cataplexy: sudden, brief (seconds to minutes) loss of bilateral muscle tone triggered by strong, typically positive emotions (laughter, joking, excitement, surprise); consciousness is completely preserved. 3) Hypnagogic (upon falling asleep) or hypnopompic (upon awakening) hallucinations: vivid, frightening, dream-like auditory/visual perceptions. 4) Sleep paralysis: temporary inability to execute voluntary movements or speak for seconds to minutes immediately upon awakening or falling asleep.
high_yield_pearl: Narcolepsy tetrad: Excessive daytime sleepiness + Cataplexy (emotion-triggered tone loss, intact awareness) + Hypnagogic hallucinations + Sleep paralysis.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 1: Narcolepsy MSLT Diagnosis
question: A young patient with suspected narcolepsy undergoes diagnostic sleep laboratory testing consisting of overnight polysomnography followed the next day by the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT). The MSLT measures the patient's propensity to fall asleep across five scheduled 20-minute nap opportunities spaced 2 hours apart. Which quantitative findings on the MSLT confirm the diagnosis of narcolepsy?

options.text: A mean sleep latency greater than 15 minutes and total absence of all REM sleep epochs
A mean sleep latency of less than or equal to 8 minutes and two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs)
Presence of alpha rhythm intrusion during slow-wave sleep on all nocturnal montages
An Apnea-Hypopnea Index greater than 30 events per hour with oxygen desaturations below 80%
Continuous high-voltage delta wave activity during every nap opportunity without sleep spindles

explanation: Diagnostic confirmation of narcolepsy requires an overnight polysomnogram (PSG, to rule out alternative sleep disorders such as sleep apnea and ensure at least 6-7 hours of baseline sleep) followed immediately the next day by the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT). Normal individuals take 10 to 15 minutes to fall asleep in a nap setting and enter REM sleep only after 80 to 100 minutes. In patients with narcolepsy, MSLT demonstrates: 1) Pathological sleepiness: a mean sleep latency $\le$ 8 minutes. 2) Sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs): $\ge$2 SOREMPs (REM sleep occurring within 15 minutes of sleep onset) across the 5 nap opportunities (or 1 SOREMP on MSLT plus a SOREMP on the preceding night's PSG).
high_yield_pearl: Narcolepsy MSLT criteria: Mean sleep latency $\le$ 8 minutes + $\ge$ 2 Sleep-Onset REM Periods (SOREMPs).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 1: Narcolepsy Pharmacology
question: A 22-year-old woman is diagnosed with Narcolepsy Type 1. Her treatment plan must address both her severe daytime somnolence and her frequent, disabling cataplectic attacks triggered by laughter. Which combination of pharmacotherapies is standard first-line management for these two distinct symptom domains?

options.text: Oral haloperidol for daytime sleepiness, and oral bromocriptine for cataplexy
High-dose oral diazepam for daytime sleepiness, and intravenous levetiracetam for cataplexy
Modafinil (or solriamfetol) for daytime sleepiness, and sodium oxybate (or venlafaxine) for cataplexy
Subcutaneous insulin for daytime sleepiness, and oral hydrochlorothiazide for cataplexy
Topical melatonin patches for daytime sleepiness, and oral diphenhydramine for cataplexy

explanation: Management of Narcolepsy addresses two distinct clinical targets: 1) Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS): First-line agents are non-amphetamine wake-promoting stimulants such as modafinil or armodafinil (dopamine reuptake inhibitors with low abuse potential), or solriamfetol (dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), followed by traditional stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) or pitolisant (histamine H3 receptor antagonist/inverse agonist). 2) Cataplexy: First-line therapy is Sodium Oxybate (gamma-hydroxybutyrate / GHB, administered at bedtime to enhance slow-wave sleep and suppress daytime cataplexy) or REM-suppressing antidepressants such as SNRIs (venlafaxine), SSRIs (fluoxetine), or TCAs (clomipramine), which increase noradrenergic and serotonergic tone to suppress cataplexy.
high_yield_pearl: Narcolepsy treatment: Daytime sleepiness = Modafinil / Solriamfetol. Cataplexy = Sodium oxybate (GHB) or SNRIs (venlafaxine).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 1: Cataplexy Neurophysiological Mechanism
question: During an episode of cataplexy in a narcoleptic patient, the patient's knees buckle while laughing, resulting in a gentle collapse to the floor. What neurophysiological mechanism accounts for this sudden, transient motor paralysis?

options.text: Acute profound hypokalemic metabolic shifts impairing peripheral motor axon action potential conduction across limbs
Transient generalized paroxysmal epileptic seizure discharges originating bilaterally from mesial temporal lobe structures
Emotional activation of the amygdala drives aberrant daytime recruitment of the brainstem REM sleep muscle atonia circuit
Sudden autoimmune autoantibody binding to neuromuscular junction nicotinic receptors inducing flaccid muscle weakness
Acute bilateral ischemic stroke involving corticospinal tract axons traversing the posterior limbs of internal capsules

explanation: Cataplexy represents the intrusion of REM sleep muscle atonia into awake consciousness. Under normal conditions, orexinergic projections from the lateral hypothalamus stabilize brainstem motor circuits against emotional disinhibition. In narcoleptic patients who lack orexin, strong emotions (processed in the limbic system, particularly the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex) send aberrant excitatory projections to the sublaterodorsal (SLD) nucleus in the pons. The SLD immediately activates glycinergic and GABAergic inhibitory interneurons in the ventromedial medulla, hyperpolarizing spinal alpha motor neurons and producing sudden, flaccid skeletal muscle paralysis identical to normal REM sleep atonia, while cortical consciousness remains fully intact.
high_yield_pearl: Cataplexy mechanism: Emotional limbic (amygdala) stimulation triggers REM-sleep muscle atonia (SLD glycinergic pathway) during wakefulness due to lack of orexin.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 2, 6: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD)
question: A 68-year-old retired naval officer is brought to the sleep clinic by his wife because of violent nighttime behavior. For the past two years, he thrashs, shouts obscenities, punches the air, and kicks violently in his sleep. Last week, he leaped out of bed and tackled a dresser, believing in his dream that he was defending himself against hostile intruders. When awakened, he is instantly alert and vividly recounts the combative dream. Polysomnography during REM sleep shows prominent, sustained skeletal muscle tone on the submental EMG. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Sleep terror disorder (night terrors) occurring during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep
Confusional arousals resulting from severe sleep deprivation and obstructive sleep apnea
Nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy causing hypermotor seizures during wake-sleep transitions
Dissociative fugue state triggered by underlying post-traumatic stress disorder
REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) caused by degeneration of brainstem pathways that mediate REM muscle atonia

explanation: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by the loss of normal skeletal muscle atonia (paralysis) during REM sleep, allowing patients to physically 'act out' their dreams (often vivid, unpleasant, action-filled, or violent dreams involving being attacked or pursued). Patients exhibit complex motor behaviors: punching, flailing, kicking, shouting, and leaping from bed, frequently causing significant traumatic injury to themselves or their bed partner. Unlike Non-REM sleep terrors, when awakened from RBD, the patient is immediately alert, coherent, oriented, and can vividly recall the dream scenario.
high_yield_pearl: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD): Loss of REM atonia $\rightarrow$ patients act out violent dreams. Immediately alert when woken with vivid dream recall.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 6: RBD & Alpha-Synucleinopathies
question: A 70-year-old man diagnosed with REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is counseled regarding the long-term prognosis of his condition. The physician explains that RBD is a powerful, highly specific prodromal marker for a particular category of neurodegenerative diseases. Which group of disorders is this patient at exceptionally high risk of developing over the next 10 to 15 years, and what is the first-line medication for symptom management?

options.text: Prion protein diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and Kuru); managed with high-dose intravenous amantadine
Trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders (Huntington disease and spinocerebellar ataxias); managed with tetrabenazine
Tauopathies (Alzheimer disease and Frontotemporal lobar degeneration); managed with donepezil
Alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, Multiple System Atrophy); managed with low-dose clonazepam or melatonin
Motor neuron diseases (Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy); managed with riluzole

explanation: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is the strongest known clinical prodromal marker for the $\alpha$-synucleinopathies: Parkinson's Disease (PD), Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), and Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). Longitudinal studies demonstrate that over 80% of patients with idiopathic RBD eventually phenoconvert to an overt $\alpha$-synuclein neurodegenerative disorder within 10 to 15 years. The underlying pathology is early Lewy body / $\alpha$-synuclein deposition in the lower brainstem tegmentum (specifically the sublaterodorsal nucleus and pedunculopontine area) prior to nigrostriatal or cortical involvement. First-line pharmacotherapy for RBD is bedtime low-dose clonazepam (a long-acting benzodiazepine) or high-dose melatonin, along with environmental bedroom safety modifications.
high_yield_pearl: RBD is a prodromal marker for $\alpha$-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's, Lewy Body Dementia, MSA) in >80% of cases. Treat: Clonazepam or Melatonin + bedroom safety.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 3, 5: Sleep Terrors vs. Nightmares
question: A 6-year-old boy is brought by his parents because of terrifying nighttime episodes. Approximately 90 minutes after falling asleep, he abruptly sits bolt upright in bed screaming incoherently, with wide eyes, sweating, dilated pupils, and a heart rate of 140 bpm. His parents are unable to comfort or awaken him. After 10 minutes, he lies back down and falls asleep. The next morning, he has complete amnesia for the episode. In contrast, an 8-year-old girl wakes up at 5:00 AM crying from a scary dream about a monster, runs to her parents' bedroom, is fully alert, and vividly describes the dream. Which sleep stages do these two conditions represent?

options.text: Sleep terrors occur during relaxed wakefulness; nightmares occur during Stage N2 Non-REM sleep
Sleep terrors occur during active REM sleep; nightmares occur during Stage N2 sleep spindles
Both conditions occur exclusively during Stage N3 sleep but represent different degrees of emotional maturity
Sleep terrors occur during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; nightmares occur during Stage REM sleep
Sleep terrors occur during Stage REM sleep; nightmares occur during Stage N1 Non-REM sleep

explanation: Sleep Terrors (Night Terrors) and Nightmares are classic pediatric parasomnias distinguished by sleep stage and clinical features: 1) Sleep Terrors: Non-REM parasomnia occurring during Stage N3 Slow-Wave Sleep, typically during the first third of the night. Features: abrupt awakening with a piercing scream, intense autonomic arousal (tachycardia, diaphoresis, tachypnea, mydriasis), child is inconsolable and unresponsive to comforting, and has COMPLETE AMNESIA for the event upon waking in the morning. Reassurance is primary. 2) Nightmare Disorder: REM parasomnia occurring during Stage REM sleep, typically in the second half or last third of the night. Features: vivid, frightening dream content; upon waking, the child is immediately fully alert, oriented, easily consoled, and VIVIDLY RECALLS the dream.
high_yield_pearl: Sleep Terrors = Stage N3 Non-REM (first 1/3 of night, scream, autonomic arousal, inconsolable, AMNESIA). Nightmares = Stage REM (late night, alert, REMEMBERS dream).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 5: Sleepwalking (Somnambulism)
question: A 10-year-old boy is found by his parents walking downstairs in the middle of the night 2 hours after bedtime. His eyes are open with a glassy, blank stare. When spoken to, he mumbles unintelligibly, walks into the kitchen, opens the refrigerator, and then allows himself to be guided back to bed without waking up. The next morning, he has no recollection of the event. During which sleep stage did this episode originate, and what is the primary management recommendation?

options.text: Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; managed primarily with environmental safety precautions and avoiding sleep deprivation
Stage REM sleep; managed first-line with immediate initiation of long-term scheduled high-dose antiepileptic medications
Stage N1 light sleep; managed with urgent stereotactic neurosurgical ablation of hyperactive mesial temporal amygdaloid nuclei
Stage N2 sleep spindles; managed with continuous positive airway pressure mask ventilation and supplemental nocturnal oxygenation
Wake-sleep transition state; managed with high-dose dopamine receptor antagonist medications and daytime psychostimulant therapy

explanation: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a Non-REM arousal parasomnia that arises from Stage N3 Slow-Wave Sleep, most commonly occurring during the first third of the night when N3 sleep is most abundant. It involves complex, semi-purposeful motor behaviors (such as sitting up, walking around the house, dressing, or eating) executed during deep sleep. Patients have open eyes with a blank stare, impaired responsiveness, and difficulty being awakened; they exhibit complete morning amnesia. Precipitating factors include sleep deprivation, fever, stress, and obstructive sleep apnea. Primary management is environmental safety (locking doors and windows, removing bedroom obstacles/cords, gate at stairs) and reassurance, as most children outgrow it by adolescence.
high_yield_pearl: Sleepwalking (Somnambulism): Stage N3 Non-REM parasomnia (first 1/3 of night). Blank stare, unarousable, morning amnesia. Management = bedroom safety & sleep hygiene.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2, 5 & Content Q1: Nocturnal Enuresis
question: A 7-year-old boy has primary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting at least 3 nights per week without ever achieving 6 continuous months of nighttime dryness). Physical examination and urinalysis are normal. During which sleep stage does enuresis most commonly occur, and what is the most effective first-line behavioral and pharmacologic treatment strategy?

options.text: Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; managed first-line with an enuresis moisture alarm, followed by oral desmopressin if needed
Stage N1 light sleep; managed first-line with central nervous system psychostimulants like oral methylphenidate taken at bedtime
Stage REM sleep; managed first-line with continuous positive airway pressure mask ventilation and supplemental nighttime oxygen
Awake quiet rest; managed first-line with high-dose loop diuretics like oral furosemide administered immediately before sleep
Stage N2 sleep spindles; managed first-line with bilateral sacral nerve root surgical rhizotomy to denervate the detrusor muscle

explanation: Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) is involuntary urination during sleep in a child $\ge$5 years of age. It most frequently occurs during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep (and N2), reflecting a mismatch between nocturnal urine production, bladder functional capacity, and central arousal mechanisms (the child fails to wake up to bladder stretch signals). Management: 1) First-line behavioral therapy: motivational therapy and an enuresis moisture alarm (the most effective long-term therapy with the lowest relapse rate; conditions the child to wake to bladder fullness). 2) First-line pharmacotherapy (for rapid, short-term relief, e.g., for camp or sleepovers): Desmopressin (DDAVP, a synthetic V2 vasopressin agonist that increases water reabsorption in renal collecting ducts, reducing nocturnal urine volume).
high_yield_pearl: Nocturnal Enuresis: Stage N3 Non-REM sleep. First-line behavioral = Enuresis alarm. First-line medication = Desmopressin (DDAVP, V2 agonist).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 4: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
question: A 52-year-old obese man (BMI 36 kg/m2, neck circumference 18.5 inches) presents with severe daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and dry mouth. His wife reports that he snores loudly and periodically stops breathing during sleep for 20 to 30 seconds, followed by a loud, gasping snort that wakes her up. Laboratory testing reveals polycythemia (hematocrit 56%) and systemic hypertension (155/95 mmHg). What is the fundamental anatomical and physiological mechanism of this disorder?

options.text: Transient cessation of central medullary rhythmic respiratory drive resulting from bilateral phrenic motor neuron demyelination and axonal atrophy
Severe episodic bronchospasm and dynamic expiratory small airway collapse mediated by massive inflammatory leukotriene hypersecretion in lung airways
Chronic restrictive alveolar hypoventilation caused by severe advanced ankylosing spondylitis fusion across all thoracic costovertebral facet joints
Autoimmune antibody destruction targeting carotid body peripheral oxygen chemoreceptor glomus cells, abolishing central hypoxic ventilatory drives
Repetitive collapse and occlusion of the upper pharyngeal airway during sleep due to loss of dilator muscle tone against negative inspiratory pressure

explanation: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is characterized by repetitive episodes of partial (hypopnea) or complete (apnea) collapse of the upper pharyngeal airway during sleep. Factors predisposing to collapse include excess pharyngeal adipose tissue (obesity, thick neck), craniofacial retrognathia, enlarged tonsils, and the physiological relaxation of pharyngeal dilator muscles (particularly the genioglossus, innervated by CN XII) during sleep onset. Inspiratory negative intrathoracic pressure sucks the floppy airway walls shut, causing airflow cessation despite persistent, vigorous thoracic and abdominal respiratory efforts. The resulting nocturnal hypoxemia and hypercapnia trigger autonomic sympathetic surges (causing hypertension) and stimulate renal erythropoietin secretion (causing secondary polycythemia).
high_yield_pearl: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA): Pharyngeal airway collapse despite persistent respiratory effort $\rightarrow$ hypoxia, micro-arousals, daytime somnolence, hypertension, polycythemia.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 4: OSA Polysomnography & CPAP
question: A patient with loud snoring, daytime hypersomnolence, and witnessed apneas undergoes an overnight polysomnogram. The study calculates the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). Which threshold confirms the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea, and what is the gold-standard, first-line therapy that pneumatically splints the pharynx open?

options.text: An AHI of $\ge$ 5 events per hour with symptoms (or $\ge$ 15 without); treated first-line with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
An AHI of $\ge$ 1 event per hour regardless of daytime manifestations; treated first-line with emergency bilateral permanent tracheostomy
An AHI of $\ge$ 100 events per hour during Stage REM sleep; treated first-line with high-dose respiratory stimulants such as oral theophylline
An AHI of $\ge$ 50 events per hour on polysomnography; treated first-line with radical surgical uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in all adult patients
An AHI of $\ge$ 30 events per hour with severe arterial desaturation; treated first-line with nocturnal low-flow supplemental nasal oxygen alone

explanation: The diagnosis of OSA is confirmed by overnight polysomnography demonstrating an elevated Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep). Diagnostic criteria: AHI $\ge$ 5 events/hr in the presence of symptoms (daytime somnolence, fatigue, snoring, witnessed apneas, hypertension), or AHI $\ge$ 15 events/hr regardless of symptoms. (Severity: mild 5-14, moderate 15-29, severe $\ge$30). The gold-standard first-line treatment is Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). CPAP delivers a continuous column of pressurized room air via a nasal or full-face mask, acting as a 'pneumatic stent' that prevents the soft palate, tongue, and lateral pharyngeal walls from collapsing during inspiration.
high_yield_pearl: OSA diagnosis: AHI $\ge$ 5/hr with symptoms (or $\ge$ 15/hr). Gold standard treatment = Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Central Sleep Apnea & Cheyne-Stokes
question: A 72-year-old man with severe ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 22%) undergoes polysomnography for daytime fatigue. The study demonstrates cyclical episodes characterized by a gradual crescendo-decrescendo pattern of tidal breathing separated by 25-second periods of complete airflow cessation during which there is NO thoracic or abdominal respiratory effort. What type of sleep-disordered breathing does this patient have, and what mechanism drives it?

options.text: Sleep-related hypoventilation syndrome caused by progressive bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis secondary to motor neuron anterior horn degeneration
Central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing, driven by delayed circulatory time and heightened chemoreceptor sensitivity to carbon dioxide
Obstructive sleep apnea with pharyngeal airway soft tissue collapse occurring despite persistent, vigorous thoracoabdominal diaphragmatic efforts
Severe inspiratory stridor caused by bilateral vocal cord adductor paralysis secondary to surgical recurrent laryngeal nerve traumatic transections
Catathrenia characterized by prolonged, monotonic expiratory vocal cord groaning accompanied by bradypnea during deep Stage REM sleep cycles

explanation: Central Sleep Apnea (CSA) is characterized by temporary cessation of respiratory effort due to loss of central ventilatory drive from the medullary respiratory centers (unlike OSA, there is NO respiratory effort during the apnea). Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a unique form of CSA classically seen in severe congestive heart failure (and stroke): prolonged circulation time (due to low cardiac output) delays the transport of arterial blood gases from the lungs to the central chemoreceptors. When PaCO2 rises, hyper-responsive chemoreceptors trigger severe hyperventilation (crescendo); this drives PaCO2 below the 'apneic threshold', causing central cessation of all respiratory drive (apnea, decrescendo) until PaCO2 re-accumulates, repeating the cycle.
high_yield_pearl: Central Sleep Apnea / Cheyne-Stokes: NO respiratory effort during apnea. Crescendo-decrescendo breathing in heart failure (delayed circulation time + chemoreceptor overshooting).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome
question: A 56-year-old man with extreme obesity (BMI 44 kg/m2) is evaluated for chronic dyspnea, somnolence, and ankle edema. An arterial blood gas drawn while breathing room air at rest during the DAY demonstrates: pH 7.36, PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, and serum bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. Polysomnography demonstrates frequent obstructive events. What condition is defined by this awake daytime hypercapnia in an obese patient, and how does the body compensate?

options.text: Idiopathic central sleep apnea; total suppression of renal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome); renal retention of bicarbonate buffers chronic respiratory acidosis
Metabolic ketoacidosis; respiratory hyperventilation through rapid Kussmaul respirations
Primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis; severe metabolic lactic acidosis with anion gap elevation
Pure uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea; acute respiratory alkalosis with urinary potassium excretion

explanation: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS, historically called Pickwickian syndrome) is clinically defined by the triad of: 1) Obesity (BMI $\ge$ 30 kg/m2), 2) Daytime awake alveolar hypoventilation resulting in hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg), and 3) Hypoxemia (PaO2 < 70 mmHg), in the absence of other primary causes of hypoventilation (such as severe COPD or neuromuscular disease). Approximately 90% of patients with OHS have co-existing severe OSA. The massive chest wall and abdominal mass load increase the work of breathing; blunted central respiratory drive fails to compensate. The kidneys compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis by retaining bicarbonate (elevated HCO3- >27 mEq/L).
high_yield_pearl: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian): BMI $\ge$ 30 + Awake DAYTIME hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) + Hypoxemia. Renal retention of HCO3- buffers acidosis.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 5: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
question: A 38-year-old woman presents with distressing sensations in both of her lower legs. She describes an uncomfortable 'creeping, crawling, and pulling' feeling deep within her calves that occurs exclusively when she is resting or lying in bed in the evening. She feels an overwhelming, irresistible urge to move her legs, and pacing around the bedroom or shaking her legs temporarily relieves the discomfort. What is the diagnosis, and which laboratory parameter must be screened?

options.text: Restless legs syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease); serum ferritin must be measured to evaluate for iron deficiency
Deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity; plasma D-dimer and venous duplex ultrasound must be performed
Acute compartment syndrome; intracompartmental needle pressure must be measured urgently
Intermittent neurogenic claudication; lumbar spine MRI must be obtained to assess spinal stenosis
Peripheral diabetic polyneuropathy; fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c must be checked

explanation: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS, Willis-Ekbom disease) is a common sensorimotor disorder characterized by four essential diagnostic criteria: 1) An irresistible urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable paresthesias/dysesthesias deep in the limbs. 2) Symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity (sitting or lying down). 3) Symptoms are partially or totally relieved by movement (walking, stretching, rubbing) for as long as the movement continues. 4) Symptoms are worse or occur exclusively in the evening or at night (circadian pattern). Pathophysiology involves central dopaminergic dysfunction and central iron deficiency in the substantia nigra. All patients must have their serum ferritin checked; iron deficiency (ferritin <50-75 ng/mL) is a key reversible trigger.
high_yield_pearl: Restless Legs Syndrome: Urge to move legs at rest in evening, relieved by movement. Linked to CNS iron deficiency; check serum ferritin (supplement if <50-75 ng/mL).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 5: Restless Legs Syndrome Pharmacology
question: A 45-year-old man with restless legs syndrome whose serum ferritin is normal (110 ng/mL) continues to experience severe nightly symptoms that prevent him from falling asleep. What are the two primary first-line classes of pharmacotherapy used for restless legs syndrome, and what major complication can occur with chronic dopamine agonist use?

options.text: First-generation sedating antihistamines or tricyclic antidepressants; both classes carry a high clinical risk of precipitating lethal serotonin syndromes
